entries.title: Ex-Blackhawks defenseman Seth Jones isn't exactly welcomed back, has no hard feelings
entries.summary: <p>Defenseman <b>Seth Jones</b> wasn’t exactly welcomed back Sunday to the United Center, where he played his first game since the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> traded him to the Panthers on March 1, 2025. There was no video tribute and no cheers for Jones, who badly wanted out of Chicago when the going got rough.</p><p>The deal has worked out for both sides. The Panthers got a quality player, and the Hawks got a quality goalie in <b>Spencer Knight</b>, who has stabilized the position. The Hawks also got a first-round draft pick, one of three they have in 2027.</p><p>Former Hawks general manager <b>Stan Bowman</b> had big plans for Jones after acquiring him in a draft-day blockbuster in 2021 and signing him to an eight-year, $76 million contract. Jones was supposed to take over for <b>Duncan Keith</b> as the Hawks’ top defenseman. But almost halfway through the contract, his frustration with all the losing became too much.</p><p>Still, Jones said he has ‘‘nothing but love’’ for the organization.</p><p>‘‘Had an experience here for four years,’’ said Jones, who missed the Panthers’ visit to Chicago last season because of a broken collarbone. ‘‘I like where I’m at now, but I wish this organization nothing but the best.</p><p>‘‘It was a good trade for both sides. I’m sure they’ll be very successful in the future when all these picks grow up and get more experience. It was awesome to be back for the first time.’’</p><p>Jones assisted on the Panthers’ second goal, a power-play goal, giving him 11 assists and 12 points for the season, both second on the team. He also logged 24 minutes, 55 seconds of ice time, more than anyone in the game, and put a team-high-tying four shots on goal.</p><p>On the goal, which gave the Panthers a 2-1 lead in the first period, Jones skated into the high slot with the puck and shot it toward the net. It probably would have gone wide, but it deflected in off <b>Matthew Tkachuk</b>.</p><p>‘‘I had so much time, I was kind of shocked,’’ Jones said. ‘‘I was just trying to get it in there. Sometimes you need those.’’</p><h3>Forsling returns, too</h3><p>Jones wasn’t the only former Hawks defenseman on the ice. <b>Gustav Forsling</b>, who played for the team in 2016-19, has turned into a shutdown defenseman for the Panthers, helping them to back-to-back Stanley Cup titles in 2024 and 2025.</p><p>But the Hawks weren’t the only ones who gave up on Forsling. The Canucks drafted him in 2014 and traded him to the Hawks the next year. The Hawks traded him to the Hurricanes, who put him on waivers in 2021. That’s when the Panthers claimed him.</p><p>‘‘Gustav was a late developer,’’ Panthers coach <b>Paul Maurice</b> said. ‘‘He just had to put some size on his frame, and he became so focused on his fitness and his size. He worked himself into being an NHLer. We’re lucky on that one, getting a player like that.’’</p><p>Forsling played 23:12, including a team-high 6:23 short-handed. He helped the Panthers kill all seven Hawks power plays.</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>Having played one of the toughest schedules in the league to start the season, the Hawks finally will face an opponent in their weight class Tuesday, when the Kings come to town. Both teams have six points. It will be the second of back-to-back games for the Kings, who visit the Rangers on Monday.</p><p>• Before the game, the Hawks honored defenseman <b>Ian Cole</b> for playing in 1,000 career games, a milestone he reached Friday. In 17 NHL seasons, he has 233 points (38 goals) and won Stanley Cups with the Penguins in 2016 and ’17.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Blackhawks' frustrations mount as breakdown leads to third straight loss
entries.summary: <p>Nothing is going right for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>. They certainly haven’t helped themselves much during a frustrating start to the season, but they haven’t been lucky, either.</p><p>Case in point: Ryan Donato. He had five prime scoring chances Sunday against the Panthers and didn’t convert any. Among them, he couldn’t push a sliding puck into an open net in the first period, and his stick broke after he was set up perfectly in the third.</p><p>The Hawks also couldn’t capitalize on Frank Nazar’s partial breakaway or Cole Smith’s breakaway from the red line, both in the third period. And they allowed the winning goal with 2:23 left after a bad change, falling to the Panthers 3-2.</p><p>The player responsible for the screw-up was defenseman Kevin Korchinski, who otherwise played well in his first game back after being scratched for seven in a row.</p><p>After getting a boost from Connor Bedard’s return and winning his first two games back, the Hawks have lost three in a row and have fallen to 3-8. Their schedule has been a gauntlet, and they’ve had their top forward (Bedard) and top defenseman (Bowen Byram) in the lineup for one game. But the promise of last season and the return of Patrick Kane haven’t yielded positive results.</p><p>‘‘There’s going to be frustration; we’re 3-8,’’ Bedard said. ‘‘You’ve got to use that in the next game and try to dig ourselves out. When you play with that edge, you play a little better. If we can do that the rest of the year, that’d be great.’’</p><p>Scoring would help. The Hawks have three goals during their skid. And for all the excitement surrounding Kane, he has one goal and a team-worst minus-13 plus/minus. He’s on the Hawks’ five-forward power-play unit, an experiment that hasn’t exactly worked. Overall, the power play went 0-for-7 against the Panthers.</p><p>‘‘The power play is mirroring our five-on-five game: We can’t score,’’ coach Jeff Blashill said. ‘‘I can’t say that we don’t get any chances; I think we do. Power plays are funny animals. You can get [lousy] power plays and score and good power plays not.</p><p>‘‘We’re just not scoring easy at all, and we have really good players that are going to score goals that are not scoring.’’</p><p>Shooting would help. The Hawks put 21 shots on net, right at their average. And when they did that, good things tended to happen. Ryan Greene opened the scoring with his first goal of the season. Korchinski shot the puck wide, but it went off the boards to Andrew Mangiapane, who passed to Greene in front of the net.</p><p>The Hawks veritably peppered Panthers goalie Akira Schmid with a whopping nine shots in the second period. One went in when Roman Kantserov took a pass from Kane in the right circle and beat Schmid to tie the score at 2.</p><p>The game appeared headed to overtime until the Hawks’ change went bad. Aaron Ekblad sent a pass from the Panthers’ own end to Lars Eller at the Hawks’ blue line. Eller skated in and beat Spencer Knight to his blocker side.</p><p>‘‘He’s going to want the change back,’’ Blashill said of Korchinski. ‘‘But I thought he played solid in that pair with [Sam Rinzel]. Both of them did a lot of good things. It’s unfortunate that he had the tough change.</p><p>‘‘I thought we did a lot of good things through the majority of the game. I thought the last half of the first [period] was the only time I didn’t like us at all. That was the only time I thought we got pushed around. But we came back out in the second. I thought [we] had great pushback in terms of competing. I thought we had great, great compete.’’</p><p>That hasn’t been enough, however.</p>

entries.title: 1 critically wounded in Little Village shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 23-year-old man was critically wounded in a shooting Sunday morning in Little Village, Chicago police said.</p><p>The shooting victim was outside along the 3100 block of West Cermak Road at about 10:25 a.m. when two people approached him on foot before a physical altercation took place, police said.</p><p>The 23-year-old, who police said has a valid concealed carry license and firearm owner’s identification card, pulled out a gun and fired toward the assailants, according to police.</p><p>One of them was shot and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in critical condition. No other injuries were reported, police said.</p><p>Area 4 detectives were speaking with a person of interest.</p>

CTA, Metra and Pace to decide on fares, control construction projects and set rail and bus service. The point is to make those areas more desirable places to walk, live, work and shop. The NITA Act grants the agency power to buy and develop land for reasons unrelated to transit, one expert said.</p><p><b>Zooming in</b>: The law gives NITA sweeping powers to build on land near transit. It allows NITA to undertake public-private partnerships, called joint developments. "I’m exhausted but so grateful."</p><p>Last month, the jazz chanteuse and professionally trained chef and her wife, Monica Haslip, opened their newest spot, the Hunt, at the Reva and David Logan Center for the Arts on University of Chicago's campus. It's named for the late <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydidkliy-l-th/" target="_blank" >Chicago artist and sculptor Richard Hunt</a>, whose works are seen on the South Side.</p><p>The Hunt builds off Wright and Haslip's other business, Carver 47 Food & Wellness Market at Little Black Pearl Art & Design Center.</p><p>Opening the doors to the Hunt came just three days before Wright released her latest album, "Nearness," a collection of standards and spirituals. entries.title: Second man dies following shootout at West Garfield Park gas station
entries.summary: <p>A second man has died after a shootout late Saturday at a West Garfield Park gas station late Saturday night, Chicago police said.</p><p>Antwon McCollum, 28, an unidentified 30-year-old man and another 28-year-old man were at the gas station in the 400 block of South Kostner Avenue around 10 when a white SUV pulled up and three armed men got out and started firing shots at them, according to police. The gunmen then returned to the car and fled the scene. </p><p>The still-unidentified 30-year-old was shot in the neck and pronounced dead at Mount Sinai Hospital and McCollum was pronounced dead at 5:28 a.m. Sunday at Mount Sinai Hospital, police said. </p><p>Another 28-year-old man was shot in the knee and taken in good condition to Stroger Hospital.</p><p>Police have not announced any arrests. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Woman hit by CTA bus in Lincoln Park critically hurt
entries.summary: <p>A woman was found lying in the road after a CTA bus hit her Sunday night in Lincoln Park on the North Side. </p><p>Police found the woman, 40, just after 9 p.m. in the 2500 block of North DuSable Lake Shore Drive after a CTA. bus hit her, Chicago police said. </p><p>She was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital where she was in critical condition, police said. </p><p>There are no citations issued and the the Major Accident Unit is investigating the circumstances surrounding the crash.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man, 26, gunned down in Greater Grand Crossing
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot Sunday night in Greater Grand Crossing on the South Side. </p><p>Around 9:40 p.m., a 26-year-old man was on the sidewalk in the 7000 block of South Eberhart Avenue when he was shot multiple times in the body, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he died, police said. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Livestream execution plans may pushed more Americans to rethink death penalty
entries.summary: <p>What if President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s push for more executions ends up helping America abolish the death penalty?</p><p>After this wild October, the question is not so far-fetched.</p><p>Hegseth wanted Americans to watch the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of murdering 13 people at Fort Hood. But some of the sharpest objections came from conservatives.</p><p>Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., called streaming the execution “beyond disgusting,” adding: “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do.” Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, warned, “A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b90000" name="module-b90000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos <a class="Link" href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/wide-majority-americans-oppose-livestreaming-nidal-hasans-execution/story?id=137263671" target="_blank" >poll</a> found 80% of Americans opposed the broadcast, including 64% of Republicans. Trump canceled the livestream on Oct. 15. The execution itself remains scheduled.</p><p>That distinction matters. Opposing a spectacle is not the same as opposing capital punishment. But look at what else happened this year.</p><p>On Oct. 20, Republican Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey commuted Toforest Johnson’s death sentence to life without parole.</p><p>Johnson was convicted of murdering a sheriff’s deputy. His conviction stands, but the local district attorney, former judges and others had questioned the evidence.</p><p>“I had concerns there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment, death,” Ivey explained. She did not declare him innocent. She recognized that execution leaves no opportunity to correct a mistake.</p><p>Then there is Ohio Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. As a state senator in 1981, he voted to restore Ohio’s death penalty. After decades as a prosecutor, attorney general, U.S. senator and governor, he called for its abolition in June.</p><p>“The moral justification I had,” DeWine said, “no longer exists.” He concluded the death penalty does not deter murder and described the toll that decades of appeals exact on victims’ families. Ohio has not executed anyone since 2018. Bipartisan repeal legislation is pending, although legislative opposition remains.</p><p>Those are not identical positions. They do, however, raise questions conservatives have particular reasons to ask: How can we distrust government with ordinary powers yet trust it never to execute an innocent person? And what does justice require when punishment becomes a spectacle?</p><p>There is also a constitutional reason to pay attention.</p><p>Fifty years ago, in Gregg v. Georgia, the Supreme Court allowed executions to resume. But the Eighth Amendment still forbids cruel and unusual punishment. In Atkins v. Virginia, the Court prohibited executing people with intellectual disabilities. In Roper v. Simmons, it prohibited executing people for crimes committed before age 18.</p><p>Both rulings considered America’s “evolving standards of decency,” including the number of states rejecting those practices and the direction of change.</p><p>Today, 23 states have abolished the death penalty. Ten more retain it but have gone at least a decade without carrying out an execution. That is 33 states — two-thirds of the country — where executions have been abolished or absent for at least 10 years.</p><p>Just three more abolition states would make a majority. That would not automatically make capital punishment unconstitutional. The Supreme Court has no simple 26-state rule. But the growing rarity of executions is evidence future justices would have to confront.</p><p>The cruelty, meanwhile, is impossible to dismiss. In September, Tennessee’s attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection failed. She survived, and Republican Gov. Bill Lee halted the state’s remaining scheduled executions pending an independent review.</p><p>September also marked 15 years since Georgia executed Troy Davis. I stood outside that prison. Seven of nine key witnesses had recanted or changed their accounts. William Sessions, FBI director under Presidents Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush, urged Georgia to stop. It did not.</p><p>I helped lead Maryland’s successful abolition campaign in 2013, making it the first state south of the Mason-Dixon Line to end capital punishment. I learned then that this cause can unite people who disagree on almost everything else: believers in redemption, skeptics of government and people determined not to risk an irreversible injustice.</p><p>Virginia became the first former Confederate state to abolish the death penalty five years ago. More executions are taking place in some states now; today’s Court may be unwilling to overturn the punishment. Hope should not be confused with certainty.</p><p>But this October brought something real: Republicans rejected an execution broadcast, one governor spared a man amid doubts, and another is asking his state to end executions altogether.</p><p>Those are not the same steps. They are steps in the same direction.</p><p>Maybe Trump and Hegseth have inadvertently done something abolitionists could not: made more Americans look squarely at what government killing means.</p><p>Fifty years after executions resumed, that may help us finally bring them to an end.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7e0000" name="module-7e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Mom isn't keen on walk down memory lane with son
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am the mother of a beautiful 30-year-old son, "Caleb," who's married, employed and happy. We have a close relationship, and he thinks Mom and Dad (married 35 years) are awesome. He was also close to his "perfect" grandma, who died recently. He adored her, and she loved and spoiled him.</p><p>What he doesn't know is Grandma was a horrific parent who left my cold, heartless dad to marry another man, breaking up the family. Mom pushed me to graduate from high school early, forcing me into college when I wasn't prepared. I failed, and then she pushed me into a marriage at 20 to an abusive man so she could be alone with her new hubby. I divorced after two years of beatings, which she knew about before the wedding. She was manipulative and selfish even into her last days, which Caleb never saw.</p><p>Now Caleb wants me to do one of those "Mom, Tell Me About Your Life" books. I don't know what to say. Telling him I was previously married will be a jolt, but the "why" questions will be tougher. I don't want to lie, but I also don't want to ruin his image of his grandma. My husband says I should tell him only the basics, but I feel that would be a lie of omission. How do I proceed? — <i>TROUBLED PAST</i></p><p><b>DEAR TROUBLED PAST:</b> I'm sorry for the loss of your mother, even though you weren't on good terms. Caleb is old enough to understand your reasons for not wanting to participate in his project. Tell him you and your mom didn't always get along, and you'd prefer to spare him the unpleasant details. If he persists, add that these memories are painful and you don't care to relive them.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I thought I was having a private conversation with my husband on my daughter's porch. My daughter overheard some negative comments I made about her through her new home security system and was extremely hurt.</p><p>I have apologized and told her it wasn't meant for her to hear. I'm forgetful at 77, and I forgot she had told me about her new security system. We've had no contact since, even though I've sent birthday cards. She has no children but convinced her sister and her sister's kids to no longer have contact with us. What can I do? — <i>BIG MOUTH IN GEORGIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR BIG MOUTH:</b> I'm sorry you didn't mention what you said that caused you and your husband to become estranged from your children and grandchildren. Why you felt it was necessary to speak disparagingly about your daughter in her own home is puzzling, unless your relationship with her was strained to begin with.</p><p>You can apologize repeatedly for hurting her feelings, but there's no guarantee she will accept it. In the future, instead of opening your mouth, remember the words of Benjamin Franklin, who said, "I will speak ill of no man, and speak all the good I know of everybody." Especially family.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Music fans rally to support Dean Schlabowske of Waco Brothers after leukemia diagnosis
entries.summary: <p>Musician and songwriter Dean Schlabowske spent nearly 40 years building an audience by returning to their towns, sharing meals and drinks after shows, and connecting with people through a common love of music.</p><p>He is now witnessing the payback. Last month, after returning from playing shows in the United Kingdom with his band the Waco Brothers, Schlabowske received a surprise medical diagnosis: Acute Myeloid Leukemia, an aggressive cancer of the blood and bone marrow that leads to heightened fatigue, shortness of breath and easy bruising.</p><p>Suddenly, his life turned upside down.</p><p>Instead of writing his next record or playing shows around town, he is now facing full days managing multiple medications, specialist appointments and chemotherapy treatments. Looming on the horizon: insurmountable medical costs, heading into the six digits.</p><p>For a musician whose income is built through touring and side jobs, both of which were no longer possible, the shift left him facing a dire outcome: “Put everything on credit cards and go bankrupt,” he said.</p><p>But then a friend in Austin, Texas, launched <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/donate-to-support-dean-and-jo-right-now?attribution_id=sl:a23b8578-708f-4e83-83f1-c2636551b681&lang=en_US&ts=1792437780&utm_campaign=fp_sharesheet&utm_content=amp30-treatment-3&utm_medium=customer&utm_source=facebook_story" target="_blank" ><u>a fundraising campaign through GoFundMe</u></a> to see if friends could help. Within a week, donors met the limit of $65,000 and it is now hovering around $80,000. Schlabowske said he does not recognize many of the donor names but suspects they all have a common trait: “They’re fans.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“You put that good karma out there for a lot of years, and it pays dividends when you need it,” said Schlabowske.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Dean Schlabowske</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“When I was super young and toured, me and the guys in the band thought it was cool to have this punk rock attitude where we were more cynical and not as outgoing and friendly, but I learned pretty quickly what you’re doing while you’re touring is creating goodwill,” he said. “You put that good karma out there for a lot of years and it pays dividends when you need it. I’m not going to lie. There are times I get pretty emotional about it.”</p><p>Schlabowske, 61, grew up in Milwaukee but moved to Chicago in 1987 where he got a job working at the legendary Wax Trax! record label. Through his noise rock band Wreck, he became a part of the city’s thriving post-punk scene for years. The trio recorded its debut EP with Steve Albini in 1990 and four years later hired Mekons co-founder Jon Langford, who had recently moved to Chicago from Wales, to produce its follow-up.</p><p>By then, Schlabowske had discovered country music and, with Langford and his fellow Welshman Tracey Dear, he formed the country punk band the Waco Brothers. The group performed its first show standing atop the bar at the Rainbo Club in Wicker Park. By 1995, the group released “To the Last Dead Cowboy,” their first recording which served as a pioneering statement for the burgeoning alternative country movement in Chicago.</p><p>With three principal songwriters — Schlabowske, Langford, and Dear — the Waco Brothers remain one of the most enduring bands out of Chicago that have tackled political and social injustice in their music for decades.</p><p>Over the years, Schlabowske released records with his side project Dollar Store and, in recent years, he collaborated with his wife, Jo Watson, who once headed the Austin band the Meat Purveyors, on playing bluegrass and honkytonk country.</p><p>Schlabowske received his diagnosis at an urgent care clinic where he went after a few weeks of feeling fatigued and nauseous. Not long after, Watson raced him to emergency care after his breath became dangerously short. After a week of procedures, he started his first round of chemotherapy. Complicating matters is the discovery of a weak heart valve that will require open heart surgery. He is commuting weekly from the couple’s Old Irving Park apartment to Lutheran General Hospital in Park Ridge.</p><p>Since his diagnosis, Schlabowske has put music on the back burner and is instead focusing on his regimen of appointments and medication, and taking a daily walk. He cannot see people for fear of an infection. At first, he had to board his two dogs, but they are expected home soon because he says he needs the emotional relief.</p><p>Despite the life change, he is taking everything in with a healthy dose of humor. “I’m 61. I’ve done a lot of cool [stuff]. Do I want to live to 100? Sure, but if that’s not meant for me, that’s not meant for me. This didn’t happen when I was 30. Any other way of looking at it leads to a dead end of depression,” he said.</p><p>Schlabowske and Watson recently relocated back to Chicago after living for a spell in Louisiana. He is insured through Watson’s job as a bookkeeper for a local business, but Schlabowske says the combination of a $10,000 deductible for this year and next, plus skyrocketing medical costs, make it not enough. </p><p>The response to the GoFundMe, he said, has been humbling, especially as he scrolls through donor names of people he knew or even briefly met five, 10, 20, 30 or more years ago. They are living proof of the community that music and audience can build together over years across cities, towns and even countries.</p><p>“A lot of those names that I don’t recognize are probably people I had a really pleasant conversation with at some point along the way,” he said. “I’ve always shied away from promoting myself. But I’m immensely grateful and incredibly touched that there are so many people who wanted to help out in such a big way. I never expected it.”</p>

entries.title: Sexual assault allegations arise from Country Thunder music festival, this time at Arizona locale
entries.summary: <p>Held each summer on the Illinois-Wisconsin border, the Country Thunder music festival has been the scene of sexual violence over the years, as young female concert-goers have come forward to say they were given alcohol and possibly knockout drugs — and then raped by men at the event.</p><p>As the Chicago Sun-Times reported earlier this year, there was at least one sexual assault reported in 2025, 2024, 2022, 2017 and 2015 at the event, which serves as a large draw for Chicago area teenagers and young adults as country music’s popularity surges in the Midwest.</p><p>Recently obtained records provide further evidence that such incidents have not been limited to the Kenosha County locale. Police have fielded reports of two possible sexual assaults involving women at the festival’s Florence, Arizona, location earlier this year.</p><p>On April 13, a 24-year-old woman went to a medical facility to report she “was possibly drugged and sexually assaulted at Country Thunder,” according to records from the Pinal County, Arizona, sheriff’s office.</p><p>Two days earlier, around 8 p.m., the woman indicated she “was near the main stage area and purchased alcohol at a white vendor tent,” according to a police report.</p><p>She “bought a White Claw and the vendor opened it in front of her,” and “she returned to where her brother and his friend were, and placed her drink on the ground while hanging out listening to music.”</p><p>“It is unknown how long the drink was out of her control before picking it back up to consume it. After finishing the drink, [NAME REDACTED] felt tired and a little out of it.”</p><p>Later, she went to buy more drinks and “on the way back to her brother, she stopped to talk to some unknown people” but does not remember much of “what occurred after that, and woke up the next morning naked in a random recreational vehicle at an unknown campground.”</p><p>Upon waking, “there were three men and a woman still partying in and outside of the RV,” according to the police reports.</p><p>“While at the RV she could recall being touched by two of the males and she could remember telling them ‘no thank you.’”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ac0000" name="image-ac0000"></a> <picture entries.title: In UK, police dogs are trained to sniff out date-rape drugs, but it's not something cops here have embraced
entries.summary: <p>Young women have reported being given what they believe were knockout drugs before being sexually assaulted at the Country Thunder music festival on the Illinois-Wisconsin border in past years, which begs the question:</p><p>How can organizers or police at the multi-day outdoor festival, or any other events, stop people from bringing in and using “roofies” or other date-rape drugs such as GHB?</p><p>There may be no single or easy answer, but overseas, police are trying a new tactic: training canines to sniff out drugs known to be used significantly in facilitating sexual assaults.</p><p>The Thames Valley Police in England have started training their dogs to identify such drugs and begun using them in patrols to not only catch offenders, but serve as a deterrent, officials said.</p><p>“These are planned offenses,” said the police department’s Sgt. Lath, who asked that his first name not be used. “So it’s really about turning the tables” on offenders, “going out and looking for them.”</p><p>Part of the aim is also to “let people know this is a new tactic,” and that “we’re out proactively,” Lath said. “We’ll quite often go into pubs and clubs.”</p><p>“The dogs have proven successful,” he said, adding they’re trained to detect an array of drugs, with the most common “spiking” substances now among them.</p><p>If an illegal substance is sniffed out, there’s “a change in behavior” with the dog that the handler watches for, Lath said.</p><p>His agency is discussing this canine program with other British police departments interested in possibly following suit.</p><p>In the United States, privacy laws and practices can differ, along with crime patterns, and police resources and priorities — and local policing agencies don’t appear to be embracing the concept, at least not yet.</p><p>“At this time, our canines do not sniff for drugs that may be used in sexual assaults,” a Chicago Police Department spokeswoman said.</p><p>“CPD’s canines are trained for various duties that include building searches for hidden offenders, locating missing persons, tracking suspects who have fled the scene of a crime, performing article searches, detecting narcotics or explosives, and conducting public service canine demonstrations.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5e0000" name="image-5e0000"></a> class="Figure-credit"><p>Thames Valley Police</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“At this time, we have approximately 60 canines.”</p><p>The Cook County sheriff’s office has about two dozen dogs, “of which a little more than half are certified by the state to detect the following four substances and their derivatives: cocaine, heroin, methamphetamines and cannabis. The first three substances are illegal with no carve outs for medical or therapeutic use, and cannabis has strict laws governing legal possession, quantity and use.”</p><p>“The sheriff’s office does not train its K9s to detect drug compounds that may be legally possessed for legitimate medical or therapeutic use. There are significant Constitutional and legal restrictions on how and when K9s may be used even when deployed to search for illegal narcotics they are certified to detect, and these restrictions would be even tighter if the substances K9s are asked to detect have legitimate legal uses.”</p><p>“Ketamine and GHB, which are two of the three drugs often considered ‘date rape’ drugs, can be legally prescribed in the U.S. The third, Rohypnol, cannot be prescribed, but is in the benzodiazepine class of therapeutic drugs and is chemically similar to Xanax, Valium, Klonopin, and other commonly prescribed drugs used to treat anxiety, sleeplessness and withdrawal.”</p><p>A spokeswoman for the Illinois State Police said: “ISP canines are not trained to detect ‘date rape drugs.’ Canines are currently focused on detecting (imprinted on) methamphetamine, heroin, cocaine and crack cocaine.”</p><p>“We are not aware of law enforcement agencies in the U.S. training and utilizing K9s to detect date rape drugs. ISP is consistently having discussions about how best to utilize the resources available to us in the pursuit of justice. Please note, ISP K9’s main jurisdiction and focus is on drug interdiction along highways and major routes across Illinois.”</p><p>The State Police has about 70 canines statewide.</p><p>Use of knockout drugs in sexual assaults has been a major concern for years. More recently, in at least one of the cases involving reports of sexual assaults at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/13/university-of-chicago-sexual-assault-alpha-epsilon-pi" >University of Chicago fraternity houses,</a> allegations surfaced that the victim drank alcohol that might have been spiked. In that case, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/21/university-chicago-sexual-assault" >a woman told Chicago police</a> she feared she was drugged before being sexually assaulted at the Alpha Delta Phi house in February.</p><p>Some experts say it’s worth exploring whether to broaden the drug menu the dogs are trained on, noting it’s not that difficult to add one or more compounds to the training mix.</p><p>Brandon Parker, founder and CEO of Rockford-based MPIK9 that trains police and security dogs, said: “Would it be effective here? Yes. Is it being used here? Not that I know of.”</p><p>He added, “It’s a good idea.”</p>

entries.title: NITA has unprecedented power to develop land near transit. How could this change your neighborhood?
entries.summary: <p>When lawmakers passed the law creating the Northern Illinois Transit Authority nearly a year ago, they spoke about the new agency’s grand mission to transform Chicago-area public transit.</p><p>To make that happen, lawmakers concentrated power in NITA that its predecessor, the Regional Transportation Authority, never had. For the first time, the umbrella agency over the CTA, Metra and Pace could set fares, control construction projects and set rail and bus service.</p><p>But, tucked inside the thousand-page-plus law, they also granted NITA unprecedented power to buy and develop land near transit.</p><p>The technical term for this is transit-oriented development, or TOD. It’s the method for building on underused land near transit to boost ridership. The point is to make those areas more desirable places to walk, live, work and shop.</p><p>For years, transit agencies in other major American cities like Washington, D.C., have had powers to develop underused, transit-owned land.</p><p>The NITA Act catches Chicago up to its peers. But it goes further by granting power to buy and develop land for reasons unrelated to transit, says Yonah Freemark, an expert on the method at the Urban Institute, a DC-based think tank.</p><p>"There are some provisions that give NITA substantial power for undertaking transit-oriented development projects itself that virtually no other transit agency across the country has,” he says. "This could be a potentially massive change."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e40000" name="image-e40000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/90c8403/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/87d90d4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/13a204f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Transit-oriented development 43G One opened in 2023 at 4308 S. Calumet in Bronzeville." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/13a204f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/738ec9e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/13a204f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Transit-oriented development 43G One opened in 2023 at 4308 S. Calumet in Bronzeville.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The law gives NITA sweeping powers to build on land near transit. It allows NITA to undertake public-private partnerships, called joint developments. The agency can take on debt, offer incentives for developers, and condemn land, so long as it has a municipality's approval.</p><p>NITA officials say they are committed to using these new powers. But there are challenges. The agency still has to create its own development office. Developing anything right now is difficult thanks to high loan and construction costs. And any NITA-led development could still be years away.</p><h3>Why do it?</h3><p>NITA’s new powers could accelerate development near transit, says Juan Sebastian Arias, who has been advocating for TOD for years as leader of downtown nonprofit Elevated Chicago.</p><p>“It’s such a huge opportunity,” Arias says. “NITA doesn't have to do this on their own. There's opportunities to partner with the city or municipalities who have their own vacant land near stations.”</p><p>There are many potential benefits. Households can potentially save up to $10,000 a year in transportation costs, according to the Chicago-based Metropolitan Planning Council. TOD <a class="Link" href="https://metroplanning.org/projects/equitable-transit-oriented-development/" target="_blank" ><u>increases access</u></a> to jobs, especially among low-income families, and can also lead to higher home values, higher retail sales, lower obesity rates and less traffic congestion with fewer people driving, the council found.</p><p>Other cities have been pushing for developing land near transit for years.</p><p>The Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority has built 10,800 new homes in the last five years. LA's Metro is working to build 10,000 homes on agency-owned land in the next five years. BART in the Bay Area has built more than 4,200 homes near transit.</p><p>The city of Chicago has been encouraging TOD since 2013, when City Council passed an ordinance removing some of the parking spot minimums for new buildings near train stations.</p><p>The city bolstered transit development again in 2021 when it passed an ETOD policy — for equitable transit-oriented development — that sought to push transit development while making sure low-income residents are not pushed out. </p><p>Since then, the city has made <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/12/chicago-progress-equitable-transit-oriented-development-5-years-policy-push-report" target="_blank" >substantial progress</a> developing city-owned land near transit, according to a May report from Elevated Chicago. More than 100 of those projects are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/12/chicago-progress-equitable-transit-oriented-development-5-years-policy-push-report" target="_blank" >underway</a>.</p><h3>Win-win development</h3><p>But as the city pushed TOD-friendly policies, Chicago's transit agencies struggled to spur development themselves.</p><p>NITA's predecessor, the RTA, could help municipalities plan development but not lead it.</p><p>"We've been doing planning studies ... <a class="Link" href="https://nita.illinois.gov/communities/community-planning" target="_blank" >for nearly 30 years</a>," says Heather Mullins, NITA's division manager for local planning. "But that's really all we could do."</p><p>The NITA Act changes that. Now, NITA is in the driver's seat. </p><p>NITA can now partner with developers to build on transit-owned land, "something we've wanted to be doing for quite some time," Mullins said.</p><p>But first, the agency must staff a new office to lead such projects. NITA is in the process of hiring a manager for that department, which will have about 10 employees, she said.</p><p>Mullins acknowledges that lawmakers have given NITA immense power to build up areas near transit, including the power to buy land. But first, Mullins says, NITA plans to build up unused land currently owned by transit agencies.</p><p>Under the law, NITA must inventory all underused transit-owned parcels and publish the list by June 2027. That list isn’t public yet. But Mullins said the agency has identified 3,000 underused parcels owned by transit agencies. She said 91 of them are ripe for development. Most of them are in the suburbs. That's enough land near transit to build 8,500 homes.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" issuing new housing permits.</p><h3>Building supercharged</h3><p>The NITA Act also overhauls a major obstacle to building cheaper, dense projects near transit: mandatory parking spot minimums.</p><p>Called People Over Parking, the new rule eliminates all municipal parking spot requirements within half a mile of a rail station, and within one city block of bus corridors.</p><p>That's key for spurring development, says Audrey Wennick, a senior director of transportation policy with the Metropolitan Planning Council.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Top movies we saw at this year’s Chicago International Film Festival: Reginald Ponder’s picks
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago International Film Festival is a movie lover’s delight, showcasing more than 100 feature films and nearly 60 short films. While it was impossible to see it all, it was possible to curate a slate of films that piqued my curiosity. In addition to special events, red carpets and interviews, I saw 19 feature films and eight short films over 12 days. Here are the films that made my top five “most” list. Each is worthy of your viewing, so keep an eye out for opportunities to see them.</p><h3>Most Galvanizing: “14th”</h3><p>This documentary by Ava DuVernay takes a look at the 14th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution and what it means to exist in the world today and to the promise that America makes to its citizens. Through a series of interviews, DuVernay connects the 14th Amendment’s origins to today’s attacks on its protections, including birthright citizenship and the right to vote. The film also addresses the clause concerning disqualification from office for insurrection or rebellion. What might feel like a lecture becomes more of a call to action to participate and protect fundamental ideals of equality and justice. DuVernay does an exceptional job of weaving together interviews, commentary by politicians, educators and even comedians, historical material and current-day footage to illustrate the relevance of this discussion and simply why we should care. Powerful, personal and promising.</p><p><i>“The 14th” will premiere worldwide on Netflix on Dec. 4, following a theatrical release in select U.S. theaters beginning Nov. 27.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1c0000" name="image-1c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/96fe2ec/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8272x4642+0+779/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2Fd4%2Fd9c019724672bd6b222809054683%2F14th-film-still-credit-paul-garnes.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/00e3680/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8272x4642+0+779/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2Fd4%2Fd9c019724672bd6b222809054683%2F14th-film-still-credit-paul-garnes.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c168bbb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8272x4642+0+779/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2Fd4%2Fd9c019724672bd6b222809054683%2F14th-film-still-credit-paul-garnes.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="14th. The documentary takes a look at the 14th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Paul Garnes/Netflix </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Most Inspiring: “Elsinore”</h3><p>This film follows the life of actor Ian Charleson, who finds himself in the middle of an opportunity and a tragedy. He has AIDS and is offered the part of Hamlet at the National Theatre of London after Daniel Day-Lewis drops out. Charleson’s struggle asks the question: Is it better to live to have life, or is it better to have life while you live, truly live? There is nothing more poignant than Hamlet’s existential investigation of “to be or not to be, that is the question.” This is a question Charleson, who died in 1990, confronts with vigor and valor. The filmmakers deliberately tie Hamlet’s plight to Charleson’s journey, elevating the play beyond a mere performance within a film. It becomes a commentary on mortality steeped in Charleson’s reality. Beautifully shot, excellently scored and personally piercing.</p><p><i>“Elsinore” will open in limited theaters Nov. 20.</i></p><h3>Most Intimate: “Once Upon a Time in Harlem”</h3><p>This film completes the work of famed filmmaker William Greaves. The documentary brings together Black luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance to discuss that time period and its impact. Greaves’ son David and granddaughter Liani embarked on the humongous task of taking hours of footage and allowing viewers to be a fly on the wall as these groundbreakers reminisced and debated what it meant to be Black and brilliant. You will laugh as they laugh, ponder as they pontificate, question as they challenge each other and marvel as they recount the memories of those who helped pave the way. “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” allows us to witness history and passes the baton for us to continue the conversation today.</p><p><i>“Once Upon a Time in Harlem” opened in theaters in October and is not available for streaming yet.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-840000" name="image-840000"></a> <picture “All of a Sudden”</h3><p>Marie, a nursing home director, struggles to convince her institution to revolutionize patient care from speed and profit to humane, self-affirming treatment. A chance encounter with Mari, a terminally ill playwright and director, sparks a bond that reshapes Marie’s quest to make the seemingly impossible possible, providing care that restores dignity and individuality.</p><p>“All of a Sudden” is loud in its protest against the mistreatment of the elderly, yet tender and quiet in the friendship and love Mari and Marie share. That bond extends to their approach to patient care. It is heartwarming to see residents viewed as people rather than profits or problems. The film asks what it truly means to live, proposing that everyone, including Mari, Marie and the elderly, deserves that chance. “All of a Sudden” is a powerful protest softened by life’s reality and affirmed through the dignity and humanity demanded by its finality. </p><p><i>“All of a Sudden” is scheduled for a U.S. theatrical release on Nov. 25.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" graduating from high school. Minnie, played by Katherine Mallen Kupferer, is Callie’s best friend who lives in the shadows of Callie’s talents and personality. A tragic accident leaves Helen and Minnie trying to find their place in this new world without Callie. Their need to stay connected to Callie in some form or fashion threatens boundaries and creates a dysfunction that is simply unsustainable. “Mouse” is an interesting exploration of grief through the eyes of both Helen and Minnie but also all the lives Callie touched. It is sad, funny and unnerving, but the range of emotions is necessary for these two to discover life after loss. Chicago directors Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson present a slice of life that feels real and thoughtful. And the lead actors bring an authenticity to the roles that says, “I know these people and I know this pain.”</p><p><i>“Mouse” in open in limited theaters Nov. 6, before expanding to wider audiences on Nov. 13.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-050000" name="module-050000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>For more film news:</h3><ul id="rte-132811b2-cc02-11f1-93e8-d7a4a3eaa479"><li>From film icons to NBA stars, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/10/15/chicago-international-film-festival-celebrity-movie-red-carpet-john-c-reilly-derrick-rose" ><u>these celebrities</u></a> are in town for CIFF</li><li>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/08/25/chicago-international-film-fest-2026-lineup-bob-odenkirk-curtis-duffy-martin-mcdonagh" ><u>2026 CIFF lineup</u></a> includes documentaries on Bob Odenkirk, chef Curtis Duffy</li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/06/25/chicago-music-box-theatre-debuts-third-screen-lakeview-movie-expansion" ><u>Chicago’s Music Box Theatre</u></a> debuted its third screen earlier this year</li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

Butter coats my tongue, and while I’ve barely reached the croissant’s tender, lacy middle, the evidence is already damning. Golden shards litter the plate and table, burrow in my clothes and between my laptop keys. What uncomplicated, chaotic bliss to demolish a plain croissant at Floriole Cafe & Bakery.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div id="Form-newsletter-wrapper" And bakeries looking to capture our fickle attention seem happy to comply.</p><p>So I set out to sample some of the dizzying bounty now at our fingertips — from traditional chocolate to flavormaxxed banana pudding, infinitely crunchy with drier middle to gently crackly with tender chew.</p><p>But what I found, after tasting a dozen plain and flavored croissants at as many bakeries, is I craved the familiarity and balance of the classics — quite literally, as I sat blissed out on a plain croissant at a Chicago bakery standby.</p><h3><b>A good foundation still matters</b></h3><p>A great croissant begins with proper technique. We can see, smell, hear and taste this most clearly in a classic croissant sans any fuss or filling, beckoning quietly alongside those glitzier behemoths. Let’s start with appearances.</p><p>Croissants should look oversized compared to their weight in your hand. Indeed, there’s unconscious wonder to lifting up a gargantuan, striped-mahogany croissant at the buzzy French newcomer Guillotine Bakery in West Town. <i>Shouldn’t this thing weigh more? </i></p><p>Greg Wade, head baker at Publican Quality Bread in West Town and Oak Park, looks for a shiny, deep-golden hue, shaded extra dark at the edges. Undefined layers may mean the dough was overproofed or proofed at too warm a temperature, translating to a dense, bready middle.</p><p>Croissants are a multiday process that starts with mixing the yeasted or sourdough-based dough, wrapping it around a solid block of butter, folding, chilling, shaping and baking it. Fewer folds means more “crispy coaty outside,” per Lou Turner, the self-taught head baker and executive chef at Milli. The darker hue in Milli’s croissants also comes courtesy of naturally occurring sugars in the bakery’s flour, which was milled by Janie’s Mill just three months before I demolished it with chaotic abandon.</p><p>It’s not just Milli embracing a trend toward incorporating local flours in addition to seasonal produce. Publican Quality Bread exclusively works with flours from Janie’s Mill, an organic grain miller in Ashkum, Illinois, and Fairbury, Illinois-based specialty grain farmer Spence Farm. Floriole uses local rye and whole wheat flours in its starters. Beneath the omnipresent butter, we should recognize nutty, earthy aromas of local flour and a buttery-rich yeastiness like chardonnay, owing to natural leavening from Publican’s 10-year-old sourdough starter.</p><p>“What I do is pretend, what if it didn’t have that flaky texture, what if it wasn’t loaded with butter, what are you left with?” said Wade. “The flavor and character of the dough.”</p><h3><b>Chicago’s post-pandemic pastry binge </b></h3><p>Historically, Chicago hasn’t exactly been a mecca for outstanding croissants. Even now, some maintain that the best laminated dough lives <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t1RBgRU0Fj0" target="_blank" ><u>outside city limits</u></a>. But the quality has risen in recent years, owing in part to the great, post-pandemic pastry department<a class="Link" href="https://www.eater.com/23554345/pastry-chefs-restaurant-jobs-own-business-cottage-food-laws?ref=bestfoodblog.net" target="_blank" ><u> dismantling</u></a> across the full-service restaurant industry.</p><p>The mass departure of so many talented pastry chefs meant some left the industry altogether; others joined or opened daytime bakeries, making their pastry prowess a bit more affordable for us hungry masses.</p><p>With such an array of choice, perhaps the basics have lost some of their luster for the general population. But to borrow from Wade, the character and flavor of the dough still mean something to me.</p><p>Back at Floriole, the shard carnage has multiplied as we near the pastry’s end. These croissants lean more toothsome than tender in their chew — unsurprising for a place known for outstanding bread. They're an ideal vessel for sandwich fillings like the satisfying hot ham and Swiss.</p><p>Ham and cheese is as classic a pairing for croissants as they come. But what’s better than butter, salt and flour, wrangled lovingly into that burnished, lined spiral? The croissant equivalent of bread and butter that, for $5, still represents something closer to everyday ritual. Turns out, I’m not alone here.</p><p>Through good times and less so, “plain is what really sells,” Holl said. </p><hr><p></p><h2><b>12 great Chicago croissants</b></h2><p>Though far from an exhaustive list, here are 12 outstanding croissants — from unfettered to flavormaxxed — worth seeking out around Chicago, as compiled by this writer and a handful of reliable, pastry-loving sources.</p><h3><b>Double chocolate croissant, </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.goodambler.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Good Ambler</u></b></a></h3><p><i>216 N. Peoria St., West Loop</i><br>This glistening, tiger-striped croissant bun is the chocoholic’s dream, the outrageous exclamation point on a laminated classic. Executive pastry chef Meg Galus starts by <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/CUnH5JVLAYq/?img_index=1" target="_blank" ><u>wrapping</u></a> chocolate croissant dough in dark-chocolate dough, which she fills with not two, but three Valrhona semi-sweet chocolate batons — just enough to make dogmatic French pastry chefs wring their hands. As Floriole’s Sandra Holl succinctly said of its inventor, “Meg <i>is</i> chocolate.”</p><h3><b>Strawberry milk croissant, </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.fatpeachbakery.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Fat Peach Bakery</u></b></a></h3><p><i>2907 S. Archer Ave., Bridgeport</i><br>Inspired by the vibrant cafes of Mexico City, wife-and-husband duo Kerrie Breuer and David Castillo opened their pint-sized bakery in 2024 with lines down the block for outstanding laminated pastries. A favorite since day one, the architectural marvel, strawberry milk croissant, takes a nostalgic cue from Nesquik’s Strawberry Quik. The brilliance of this surprisingly balanced sweet pastry lies in the puckering strawberry jam filling, which mingles with sweet, cloud-like cream beneath that shattering exterior. Damen Ave., Ravenswood</i><br>Known for over-the-top pastries like the umami-bomb longanisa-stuffed croissant with soy caramel and egg yolk, my go-to at pastry chef Justin Lerias’ popular Filipino-American shop is the sneaky-simple toasted rice croissant. This clever twist on a classic weaves toasted forbidden black and Minnesota-grown wild rice into dough, which bakes up expertly crisp-edged with a delicately tender middle. A whiff of subtle nuttiness complements the buttery tang. This beloved young shop is in the midst of an expansion into the adjacent storefront and will reopen later this fall. In the meantime, you can find Lerias’ laminated works of art at <a class="Link" href="https://www.delsurchicago.com/" target="_blank" ><u>residencies</u></a> around town.</p><h3><b>Ham and cheese croissant, </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.mindysbakery.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Mindy’s Bakery</u></b></a><b> </b></h3><p><i>1623 N. Milwaukee Ave., Wicker Park</i><br>Award-winning pastry chef Mindy Segal debuted her standalone Wicker Park bakery in 2022, drawing longtime fans of her excellent bagels and bialys and irresistibly burnished pastries. Executive pastry chef Bo Durham, who has been with Segal for well over a decade, takes the dough-wrangling reins here with classic and creative bakes worth the long but quick-moving queues. I’m a sucker for the savory creations here especially. (Think roasted onion, fromage blanc and parm bialys and kielbasa & sauerkraut croissant danish.) Western Ave., McKinley Park</i><br>Crunch-on-crunch-on-cream rather crudely encapsulates the textural jubilation of this toasty almond-flecked pastry filled with creamy, rich frangipane that all but begs for a cortado companion. Run by chef brothers Andrés and Guillermo Merlos and their mother, Olga, Cafe Consume shares a storefront with sibling vintage shop Consume Vintage Apparel, meaning you can browse for secondhand goodies once properly fueled on espresso and messy-good housemade pastries.</p><h3><b>Guava and cheese croissant, </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/panartesanalchicago/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><b><u>Pan Artesanal</u></b></a></h3><p><i>3724 W. class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Chocolate croissant, </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.floriole.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Floriole Cafe & Bakery</u></b></a></h3><p><i>1220 W. Webster Ave., Lincoln Park</i><br>The mild-mannered answer to Good Ambler’s chocoholic pastry, Floriole’s chocolate croissant earns its spot for achieving sweet-salty harmony. Because the croissant is a little extra salty, the cocoa-sweetness of the chocolate shines through. Best case: Pick one up within two hours of opening, because when the chocolate is still a bit warm, it melts into gooey harmony with the innermost ring of pastry, like the inside of a soft-baked chocolate chip cookie.</p><h3><b>Ham and cheese croissant, </b><a class="Link" href="https://badbutterchicago.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Bad Butter</u></b></a></h3><p><i>1655 W. Cortland St., Bucktown</i><br>Actor-turned pro baker Dan Koester moved from professional pastry kitchens to his home during the pandemic, hawking his sourdough creations as Dan the Baker before eventually debuting his brick-and-mortar storefront in April 2026. Bad Butter is known for creatively remixed, extra-crunchy croissants, zhuzhed into creations like Chicago-style hot dogs. Even the staple ham and cheese becomes pastry fine dining in Koester’s capable hands. The rich, flaky leaves encase sliced herbed porchetta from Tempesta Artisan Salumi, whole-grain mustard and Gruyère cheese, the latter of which melts into a cracker-crisp cheese skirt.</p><h3><b>Pain au raisin, </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/guillotinebakery/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><b><u>Guillotine Bakery</u></b></a></h3><p><i>1711 W. Chicago Ave., West Town</i><br>Open since June, this popular West Town newcomer channels Parisian baking with an edge, as its French Revolution-inspired name suggests. Boasting one of the best baguettes in town, the high-gloss pastries also lean classically French, as in pain au chocolat, plain croissants (both available in hilariously oversized, $40ish versions as well) and pain suisse with pastry cream. My go-to is the pain au raisin, a golden, buttery coil made from the same laminated croissant dough. Each layer of this crisp, chewy-tender revelation is swiped with sturdy custard studded with tangy sultana jewels.</p><h3><b>Banana pudding croissant, </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.sugarmoonchicago.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Sugar Moon Bakery</u></b></a></h3><p><i>3612 W. Wrightwood Ave., Logan Square</i><br>From owner Dina Cimarusti’s tiny Logan Square storefront, Sugar Moon slings high-concept yet rustic sweet and savory baked goods well worth the interminable lines. The staple banana pudding croissant, packing vanilla custard, just-caramelized banana, salty caramel, whipped mascarpone and vanilla-tinged crumb, is a balanced, light-yet rich textural marvel on its own. But its pastry vessel speaks just as loud via flaky, golden layers with a rustly crunch. Tip: You may have better luck on Fridays at this weekends-only shop. Regardless, plan to come early, and wait.</p><h3><b>Chocolate croissant, </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.misericordia.com/pages/hearts-flour-bakery-and-cafe" target="_blank" ><b><u>Misericordia Hearts & Flour Bakery</u></b></a><b> </b></h3><p><i>6130 N. Ravenswood Ave., West Ridge</i><br>The third chocolate croissant entry on this list, Hearts & Flour’s version suits the mornings that require an extra drizzle of indulgence. The golden, crackly exterior is squiggled with chocolate before giving way to a tender, buttery middle packed with more chocolate. While the weather cooperates, pair it with a floral, citrusy cardamom orange cold brew. In case you need another excuse to visit, this sunny cafe employs adults with developmental disabilities, matching responsibilities to unique abilities.</p><div class="Enhancement" </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Pistachio croissant,</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.obelixchicago.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Obelix</u></b></a></h3><p><i>700 N. Sedgwick St., River North</i><br>A crunchy, silken brunch fixture since this raucous neo-bistro opened four years ago, Obelix’s visually striking pistachio croissant began life as a special from then-pastry chef Antonio Incandela (now pastry chef/owner at Mariscos San Pedro). It became a brunch staple owing to its popularity. Now in the capable hands of executive pastry chef Courtney Kenyon-Snider, the green-striped, laminated dough envelops a cloud of satiny, not-too-sweet pistachio pastry cream that smacks of gelato. It’s available for pick up on weekends as part of the restaurant’s pre-order pastry program.</p>

entries.title: El desfile de Halloween Arts in the Dark regresa con 100,000 asistentes
entries.summary: <p>El desfile anual "Arts in the Dark" de Halloween se puso en marcha en la calle Balbo el sábado, atrayendo a un estimado de 100,000 asistentes con atracciones vibrantes y coloridas como un dragón que escupe fuego, alebrijes gigantes y un gusano luminoso de 60 pies.</p><p>El evento, que fue calificado por <a class="Link" href="https://10best.usatoday.com/lifestyle/best-halloween-parades-usa/" target="_blank" >USA Today</a> como "una de las mejores celebraciones de Halloween del mundo", tiene como objetivo incluir artistas de todos los ámbitos y de todos los distritos políticos de Chicago, dijeron los organizadores.</p><p>En su duodécimo año, el desfile contó con bandas marciales, grupos de baile y más de 1,000 intérpretes. Además de la inclusión de programas para jóvenes y organizaciones culturales, 11 distintas escuelas secundarias y tres universidades participaron en el evento de este año.</p><div entries.title: Walter Koenig, Ensign Chekov on original ‘Star Trek’ series, dies at 90
entries.summary: <p>LOS ANGELES (AP) — Actor Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, the youthful Russian navigator on the “ <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/star-trek-60th-anniversary-plans-lego-6cab7180bc56ddb4255c5a7fb61cb6b7" target="_blank" >Star Trek</a> ” television series and several movies, has died. He was 90.</p><p>Koenig died Monday at his home in the North Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles, talent agent Zachery McGinnis said in a statement.</p><p>In “Star Trek,” Ensign Chekov was the sole Communist-bloc member of the spaceship Enterprise bridge staff. His friendly, supportive presence showed how the rival nations (in the far-off future in which the show was set) were capable of working together.</p><p>Speaking heavily Russian-accented English, Chekov embodied stereotypical Russian personality traits, including fierce pride, love of poetry and blind loyalty.</p><p>“Star Trek” ran on NBC from 1966 to 1969 and has had an almost unprecedented afterlife as fans, or Trekkies, kept interest in the show alive.</p><p>“My heart is heavy,” Koenig’s castmate, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/george-takei-japanese-war-incarceration-book-07c2b803a951b766962ac029ce59da14" target="_blank" >George Takei</a>, said in a post on the social platform X. “Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend.”</p><p>“Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it,” McGinnis said. “Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.”</p><p>McGinnis said Koenig died surrounded by his daughter and niece.</p><p>Koenig was <a class="Link" href="https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/walter-koenig-dead-chekov-star-trek-russian-1236740088/" target="_blank" >born in Chicago</a> on Sept. 14, 1936, to Lithuanian immigrant parents. He played Chekov in seven “Star Trek” movies starting in 1979, as well as innumerable other spinoffs, including writing a “Star Trek” book, “Chekov’s Enterprise,” in 1980. The TV show has also inspired two spinoff TV series with new casts and conventions that draw thousands of fans.</p><p>He returned to the science fiction genre with occasional appearances in the syndicated 1990s TV series “Babylon 5.”</p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Police issue photo after CTA passenger battered at 95th/DanRyan Red Line stop
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are searching for a man who allegedly battered a 27-year-old CTA passenger earlier this month at a CTA Red Line station in Roseland. </p><p>The victim, who suffered minor injuries, was attacked Oct. 13 at the 95th/Dan Ryan station in the first block of West 95th Street, and police said. </p><p>In a community alert, police issued a picture of the alleged attacker, who was described as a male wearing a green hooded sweater with yellow designs, black pants and green and white gym shoes. </p><p>Anyone with information is encouraged to contact public transportation detectives at<br>312-745-4447 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com using reference RD JK449694.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Six Flags Great America’s Raging Bull to get seat belts after deadly Georgia coaster accident
entries.summary: <p>Six Flags Great America’s Raging Bull roller coaster in Gurnee will have seat belts for riders following a crash involving a similar ride at Six Flags Over Georgia, where a 42-year-old man died after being ejected from a similar coaster.</p><p>Raging Bull is one of three Six Flags roller coasters that will add seat belts, along with the Nitro ride at Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey and the Goliath at the Georgia park, a company spokesperson said Monday.</p><p>The company also says it will have independent engineers and ride inspection specialists review safety procedures across its parks.</p><p>“Our focus remains on supporting and cooperating with the ongoing state investigation while taking meaningful actions to further strengthen safety across our parks,” the spokesperson said.</p><p>No date has been set to reopen the Raging Bull ride. The ride will reopen after all of the work that's needed and the reviews to ensure its safety are completed, the spokesperson said.</p><p>Raging Bull opened in 1999. The tallest and longest roller coaster at the Gurnee amusement park, it stands 202 feet tall, spans 5,057 feet and hits speeds of up to 73 miles an hour.</p><p>In the incident Oct. 12 at Six Flags Over Georgia, an Atlanta man, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was ejected from Goliath and died, according to the Cobb County, Georgia, police, which said its preliminary findings were that indicated he struck other patrons before falling beneath the ride. Its investigation hasn't been finished.</p>
entries.author: Misha Manjuran Oberoi

entries.title: Movies with a political message among top flicks at Chicago International Film Festival
entries.summary: <p>The 62nd Chicago International Film Festival delivered an especially strong lineup this year. An impressive number of shows were sold out soon after tickets went on sale.</p><p>After watching 51 features and a handful of shorts, I've highlighted five highly recommended entries that put politics on the big screen. Most will never come back to local venues, so you will have to search and stream them online.</p><p>Among higher profile titles in the fest that will soon get theatrical runs, I definitely recommend: </div><p></p><h3>“Eight Bridges”</h3><p>Every year festival programmer Sam Flancher gets one experimental film into the lineup. This time it’s the minimalist, meditative “Eight Bridges” by James Benning, who screened his first film at the fest in 1971. Eight 10-minute shots beautifully frame bridges from coast to coast. First is San Francisco’s Golden Gate Bridge, followed by others over the Alabama River, Columbia River, Hudson River, Mississippi River, Sheyenne River and the Rio Grande Gorge. Longest is the Seven Mile Bridge in the Florida Keys. Benning frees our imagination to interpret the engineering and environment on our own, minus dialogue, voiceover or score. Mindful of patrons overstimulated by cinema and crowds, fest organizers set aside a Quiet Room at the AMC NewCity theater. The serene “Eight Bridges” itself offered one such “sensory-friendly quiet room space” to reset.</p><p><i>“Eight Bridges”</i> <i>is not available for streaming at the moment.</i></p><div indigenous Malayan spirituality in 1617 in “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors.”</p></figcaption></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>“Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors”</h3><p>Filipino writer-director-cinematographer-editor-production designer Lav Diaz offers a tragic saga of Catholic colonizers quashing indigenous Malayan spirituality in 1617. Obsessed with building a church, a Spanish priest forces converts to haul a load of costly marble through 50 kilometers of dense jungle. Notorious bandits lurk. It’s all for an altar to complete a 15-year construction effort. Many men have already died to build this church. Shot in indelible black and white, this gripping tale excels as a work of anthropological history. Last year at the festival, Diaz’s “Magellan,” starring Gael García Bernal, covered similar themes. Both films were shot in scenic Sampaloc, Quezon Province.</p><p><i>“Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” is making the film circuit rounds and is not slated for a wide theatrical release or is available for streaming at the moment.</i></p><h3>“Possible Love”</h3><p>The latest film by Lee Chang-dong is South Korea’s official Oscar entry for the best international feature film. The plot observes an upper-class woman making a documentary about survivors of a factory strike. Her focus is a working-class family in the aftermath of brutal anti-union violence. Inspired by a 2009 strike at a Korean car manufacturer, this deftly plotted drama incorporates some news footage of the clash. Besides critiquing the ethics of nonfiction directors, Lee scrutinizes class friction. Issues come to a head when the filmmaker and her husband invite her interview subjects for a weekend at their fancy summer house. Ironies and emotions erupt. “Possible Love” won the Ebert Director Award at the Toronto International Film Festival this year.</p><p><i>“Possible Love” comes to Netflix on Nov. 6.</i></p><div of the Trump administration’s Operation Midway Blitz. We see and hear him in the backseat of an unmarked black SUV talking with another young Latino man, via that ICE agent’s body-camera video. Thanks to U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis, that footage made its way into this incredible 18-minute documentary by Hyde Park native and Oscar nominee Bill Morrison. He accessed 65 minutes of ICE’s own video from seven body cameras for that day. Five neighbors on the scene shared 27 minutes of their cellphone videos.
