entries.title: Federal appeals panel considers who can fire top federal prosecutors named by judges
entries.summary: <p>Chicago’s top federal prosecutor said he serves at the pleasure of the president.</p><p>But Andrew Boutros<b> </b>didn’t take the traditional route to office. Nor did many of his peers. Rather, when President Donald Trump returned to the White House, he employed a law that eventually let federal judges appoint U.S. attorneys<b> </b>across the country —<b> </b>including Boutros.</p><p>That raises a critical question: Who gets to fire a judge-appointed U.S. attorney?</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/05/30/andrew-boutros-interim-us-attorney-chicago-judges-role-pam-bondi" >Is Chicago’s interim U.S. attorney here to stay? Judges could play an unusual role in picking top prosecutor</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>A West Coast legal fight might soon provide an answer. A 9th U.S. Circuit<b> </b>Court of Appeals panel<b> </b>in San Francisco spent nearly 90 minutes<b> </b>Friday<b> </b>considering whether to overrule a lower-court judge who<b> </b>concluded<b> </b>this month<b> </b>that “the president cannot unilaterally fire”<b> </b>such a prosecutor.</p><p>That judge got it wrong, Justice Department attorney<b> </b>Mark<b> </b>Freeman<b> </b>argued Friday. He said, “the power of a prosecutor is awesome. It brings the full power of the state against a citizen.</p><p>“That is why it is essential that the president be the one who can be blamed for it.”</p><p>But a U.S. attorney’s office is “supposed to be run by somebody who is confirmed by the Senate,” lawyer<b> </b>Donald<b> </b>Verrilli Jr. argued. That’s the judgment of Congress, he said, “and it is being evaded.”</p><p>The panel’s ruling will not be binding in Illinois. But it might offer guidance on a question that took on new relevance this summer. Local elected Democrats<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2026/06/04/trump-blanche-boutros-doj-broadview" target="_blank" >called on Boutros to resign</a> after his office was accused of misconduct in a high-profile case tied to Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>A judge is now considering whether to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/jon-seidel?p=00000198-1631-d49b-af99-df3def400000.2" target="_blank" >name a special prosecutor</a> to investigate Boutros and others for criminal contempt. The controversy revolves around a now-defunct conspiracy case Boutros’ office brought against a group of Midway Blitz protesters known as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“the Broadview Six.”</a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>Andrew Harnik/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Attorney General Todd<b> </b>Blanche<b> </b>has said the Justice Department “fully supports U.S. Attorney Boutros.”<b> </b>Blanche made that comment before he was confirmed to his job on a permanent basis.</p><p>U.S. District Chief Judge Virginia Kendall has declined to comment on the controversy, citing the judicial code of conduct.</p><p>The West Coast case was heard Friday by Judges<b> </b>Richard<b> </b>Paez, appointed by President Bill Clinton; Jay<b> </b>Bybee, appointed by President George W. Bush; and<b> </b>Jennifer<b> </b>Sung, appointed by President Joe Biden.</p><p>It’s unclear how they’ll rule, or when.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2026/06/04/trump-blanche-boutros-doj-broadview" >Trump’s acting attorney general backs Boutros amid fallout from botched ‘Broadview 6’ case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Traditionally, U.S. attorneys are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate. That hasn’t happened in Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2017/11/9/18363175/lausch-confirmed-to-be-chicago-s-next-u-s-attorney" target="_blank" >since 2017</a>,<b> </b>when the Senate confirmed<b> </b>Trump nominee John Lausch.</p><p>Instead, then-Attorney General<b> </b>Pam Bondi<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/03/28/former-prosecutor-andrew-boutros-named-chicagos-interim-u-s-attorney" target="_blank" >appointed<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>to the job</a> on a temporary basis<b> </b>in April 2025. Then, when that appointment expired<b> </b>four months later, Chicago’s federal judges <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/07/25/chicagos-federal-judges-choose-andrew-boutros-as-top-prosecutor" target="_blank" >chose<b> </b>Boutros</a><b> </b>to continue on a more permanent basis, using the same law at issue out west.</p><p>The controversy has caught the attention of former top feds from across the country, including ex-Chicago U.S. Attorney Scott<b> </b>Lassar. He and others filed a brief opposing the Trump administration’s interpretation of the law.</p><p>Lawful appointments matter, they wrote, because a prosecutor’s decisions<b> </b>carry<b> </b>“life-changing consequences.”</p><h3><b>A swift dismissal</b></h3><p>It took Trump less than an hour<b> </b>to<b> </b>fire<b> </b>Roger<b> </b>Rogoff, named<b> </b>July 15<b> </b>by judges<b> </b>in Seattle to be the top federal prosecutor<b> </b>there.</p><p>Shortly after he was sworn in, Rogoff<b> </b>learned<b> </b>by email<b> </b>that he’d been removed from the job — at the direction of the president.</p><p>Trump later sent the Senate a nominee for U.S. attorney, who has yet to be confirmed. The president also<b> </b>directed<b> </b>a former immigration judge<b> </b>to run the U.S. attorney’s office<b> </b>in the meantime.</p><p>Rogoff<b> </b>sued, arguing<b> </b>his dismissal by the president violated the law. On Oct. 1, U.S. District Judge Stanly Bastian<b> </b>agreed. In his preliminary injunction ruling, the judge<b> </b>posed the very question at issue: “Can the president fire a court-appointed U.S. attorney?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div vacancy is filled.” That’s generally been taken as a reference to Senate confirmation of a presidential nominee.</p><p>“It does not say until that person is fired by the president,” Bastian pointed class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Andrew Harnik/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Justice Department’s initial attempt<b> </b>to prosecute<b> </b>former FBI Director James Comey<b> </b>fell apart when a judge ruled that Lindsey<b> </b>Halligan<b> </b>had not properly been appointed U.S. attorney<b> </b>in Virginia<b> </b>under the law.</p><p>But the question in the Comey case revolved around who gets to choose the U.S. attorney once<b> </b>the attorney general’s initial<b> </b>120-day<b> </b>appointment<b> </b>expires. The Rogoff case<b> </b>turns on who can fire a judge-appointed U.S. attorney.</p><p>The Justice Department’s Freeman<b> </b>said a separate, but related, <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/28/541" target="_blank" >statute</a> makes things clear.</p><p>It says, “each United States attorney is subject to removal by the president.”</p><h3><b>‘The president makes a choice’</b></h3><p>Freeman argued in court filings that Bastian’s ruling was "indefensible."</p><p>It means a top federal prosecutor “may wield the core executive power of criminal law enforcement however he pleases — without accountability to anyone, without risk of removal for any cause, and without regard to whether he is insubordinate, corrupt, incompetent, or malfeasant — for the foreseeable future, unless the Senate agrees to confirm a replacement,”<b> </b>Freeman and his colleagues argued.</p><p>Verrilli reminded the appeals panel<b> </b>that no one forced the president to use the law.</p><p>“The president makes a choice,” Verrilli said. “A voluntary choice to gain the benefit of [the law] and the fact that he can basically put anybody he wants in the office for that interim period. But it comes with a constraint. The president opts into the constraint.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/07/chicago-crime-justice-department-doj-boutros-trump-midway-blitz-corruption" >After rocky first year, Chicago’s top federal prosecutor says he isn’t taking orders from Washington</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The judges asked Freeman and Verrilli about prior court rulings and the practical implications of their arguments,<b> </b>including whether judges may remove the prosecutors they appoint.</p><p>Along the way, Verrilli acknowledged<b> </b>for Judge Bybee that a judge-appointed prosecutor has the same power as one confirmed by the Senate.</p><p>“Your contention is that he just can’t be removed under [the law] even though he is identical in authority, power and title?” Bybee asked.</p><p>That’s correct, Verrilli argued. Otherwise, the framework of the law has “basically unraveled,” he said.</p><p>“Congress made a judgment,” he told the panel, “that this is an office that should be subjected to the advice and consent power.”</p>

entries.title: Last mayoral candidates file signatures for 2027 ballot in bid to deprive Johnson a second term
entries.summary: <p>Thirteen candidates will vie for the right to deny <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/13/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-announcement-reelection-bid-2027" >Brandon Johnson</a> a second term and become Chicago’s 58th mayor, but only if they can survive cutthroat petition challenges that could narrow the field considerably.</p><p>Joining the mayoral field on the final day of filing were: retiring Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza with a self-reported 26,000 signatures; cardiologist and political newcomer Lisa Nee with what she says were 31,000 signatures; Cook County Board of Review Commissioner George Cardenas with a self-reported 31,500 signatures; and Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas with what she said was"slightly shy of" 40,000 signatures.</p><p>Also joining the mayoral field on the final day of filing were: attorney William Quinlan, businessman Joe Holberg, conservative Danielle Carter-Walters and former real estate developer Zoe Ma.</p><p>Five candidates filed their nominating petitions on the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/19/mayor-race-candidates-stacks-nominating-petitions-chicago-board-of-elections" > first day of filing:</a> Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias; lobbyist John Kelly; former Chicago Housing Authority Chair Matthew Brewer; U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley and millionaire businessman and perennial political candidate Willie Wilson.</p><p>That brings the total number of mayoral candidates to fourteen — but that is likely to change.</p><p>Campaign managers and veteran political operatives said they expect the crowded mayoral field to shrink substantially as candidates closely scrutinize each other's nominating petitions to make certain they have the required 12,500 valid signatures to remain on the ballot.</p><p>No one will be immune from those challenges no matter how it looks, or whom it might knock off the ballot. That includes Johnson, who skipped opening day and, therefore, the lottery for the top spot on the ballot. He said he filed 33,000 signatures on Friday.</p><p>That’s a relatively low number for an incumbent mayor. Richard M. Daley, Chicago’s longest serving mayor, once filed more than 100,000 signatures with help from once powerful Democratic ward organizations filled with city workers.</p><p>“I’m looking at everybody — particularly the African-American ones,” Wilson told the Sun-Times. “And if somebody do challenge me, I’m very confident that we’re OK. But that’s up to them if they want to spend the money.”</p><p>Asked whether he believes Johnson will have a problem making the ballot, Wilson said, “He’s the mayor. He’s been through this before. He ought to have his stuff in order, I would think."</p><p>The challenge period begins Tuesday and ends on Nov. 2. The adjudication of challenges will continue until Dec. 17, when the final mayoral ballot if certified.</p><p>“I know for a fact that different people have pulled Dr. Wilson’s petitions and are going through them line-to-line," said former state Sen. Ricky Hendon, who is handling petition challenges for Wilson. "The only thing I can guarantee is they can’t get him because we did the work, went down to the Board of Elections and verified the signatures before we filed them. Alice Palmer off the ballot.</p><p>“Everybody has to do the work to get on the ballot. If you don’t have the signatures, that’s a problem… That’s why they have the challenge process. Everyone is gonna be held to that scrutiny," Jubeh said.</p><p>Veteran political operative Victor Reyes, who is advising the Nee campaign, expects Giannoulias to concentrate his challenges on Quigley and others with the greatest potential to draw votes along the “vote-rich” north lakefront.</p><p>That’s where Johnson sealed his 2023 mayoral victory, and where the 2027 election is expected to be decided once again.</p><p>“You do everything you can to structure the race regardless of how they beat you up” for being the big-bucks candidate who “compromises democracy,” said Reyes.</p><p>Kelly is likely to challenge Mendoza, who is targeting the same conservative voters in Northwest and Southwest Side wards that are home to scores of police officers and firefighters. And Mendoza is likely to challenge Cardenas, the only other Hispanic in the race.</p><p>Giannoulias could challenge Kelly, Mendoza, as well as Pappas, a fellow Greek-American with whom he has a long-standing rivalry. </p><p>"He’s going for a first-round win and, with all of that money, he has the resources and the ability" to narrow the field enough to improve his chances, Reyes said.</p><p>Pappas filed her petitions wearing a shirt reading, "No biceps, just brains," a veiled jab at Giannoulias that she said "speaks for itself."</p><p>That was a reference to what she told the Sun-Times about Giannoulias on the day candidates began circulating nominating petitions. “If you want to be mayor of the city of Chicago, your IQ has to be higher than your body temperature… That’s what’s going to be required in the mayor’s race."</p><p>Pappas and Cardenas were among five candidates who filed within an hour of the deadline on Monday, thereby entering a lottery for the coveted last spot on the ballot. The others were Holberg, who said he gathered 32,000 signatures; Carter-Walters, who said she had 13,000 signatures; and Ma with a self-reported 17,000 signatures.</p>

entries.title: Illinois joins 19 other states in FTC lawsuit accusing Dollar General of false price advertising
entries.summary: <p>Illinois joined a coalition of states and Federal Trade Commission in suing Dollar General, accusing the discount chain of charging more at the checkout counter than prices advertised online.</p><p>The lawsuit alleges the company “generated millions of dollars by regularly and repeatedly charging shoppers more at the register than the prices it advertises,” in violation of both federal and state laws regarding consumer fraud, according to a statement from Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul.</p><p>“Overcharging for products at a time when many basic necessities have become less affordable harms vulnerable families and consumers,” Raoul said.</p><p>Dollar General didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>In two instances detailed in court documents, Illinois consumers were charged $0.75 to $1.78 more than was advertised online. Examples from other states allege the company charged more than four dollars above the listed price and didn’t honor coupons.</p><p>“Whatever the register rings up, that will be the price, and we can’t give you [a] discount,” an Illinois Dollar General store manager is alleged to have told a customer upset about the price differences in April 2024, per the lawsuit.</p><p>An FTC investigator who went undercover to make purchases at one location found the screens displaying the prices as items were rung up faced only the employee; in other cases, those screens were broken, according to the lawsuit.</p><p>Joining Illinois in the lawsuit are the attorneys general of Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.</p>

entries.title: Amtrak's Bridgeport railyard to get environmental review after community pressure: 'Let's keep up the fight'
entries.summary: <p>Amtrak’s new maintenance facility in Bridgeport will undergo a federal environmental review after community pushback over the project initially being allowed to move forward without one, according to the Federal Railroad Administration.</p><p>The agency’s dashboard for the project lists Oct. 8 as the start date of the environmental review, which it also said is expected to be complete by year's end.</p><p>The review will trigger a 30-day public comment period, and the federal agency said it will hold at least two public meetings on the project, though details on those have yet to be released.</p><p>Amtrak initially had received more than $600 million and a “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/what-to-know-chicago-white-sox-stadium-proposal-justin-ishbia" target="_blank" ><u>categorical exclusion</u></a>” from the federal government for the project, which allowed it to move forward without a full environmental assessment or an environmental impact statement “unless there are extraordinary circumstances.”</p><p>But the federal agency changed its tune after Amtrak said it planned to use some of the funds for the $915 million project to repair 17 viaducts “supporting the Canal Street Yard.”</p><p>“After reviewing this modified project scope, FRA has decided to prepare an environmental assessment, through a process that will include public comment, for the Proposed Action,” the agency said on its <a class="Link" href="https://www.permits.performance.gov/permitting-project/dot-projects/midwest-maintenance-facilities" target="_blank" ><u>website for the project</u></a>.</p><p>It comes after <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment/2026/10/16/amtrak-bridgeport-chinatown-justin-ishbia-white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>months of public outcry from local residents</u></a> who worry the new facility could pose health hazards, as well as generate smells and sounds that could tank property values. An initial review from the FRA determined the project would have a minimal noise, air quality and groundwater impact on the surrounding community.</p><p>Also behind neighbors' ire: the move comes hand-in-hand with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/05/jerry-reinsdorf-justin-ishbia-reach-long-term-agreement-that-establishes-a-framework-for-transition" target="_blank" ><u>potential future White Sox owner</u></a> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" target="_blank" ><u>Justin Ishbia</u></a>’s companies helping to finance Amtrak’s move while purchasing the existing rail facility, which it wants to develop as a site for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" target="_blank" ><u>proposed new stadium</u></a> for the South Side team.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/what-to-know-chicago-white-sox-stadium-proposal-justin-ishbia" >What to know about the Chicago White Sox stadium proposal</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/07/amtrak-bridgeport-rail-yard-white-sox-ishbia" >City Council grills Amtrak over proposed Bridgeport rail yard</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/10/16/amtrak-bridgeport-chinatown-justin-ishbia-white-sox" >Bridgeport, Chinatown residents tell us what they think about Amtrak rail yard development plans</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>In a joint statement Monday, Ishbia’s company, Canal Edge, and Amtrak said they welcomed the “opportunity for additional review, dialogue and feedback.”</p><p>“We believe a deeper public review process will better help stakeholders understand the need for a new facility and associated viaduct repair work as well as the environmental impact of the project,” the companies said.</p><p>Ald. Nicole Lee (11th), whose ward encompasses the proposed maintenance facility, said a 24/7 rail maintenance operation in the middle of a residential neighborhood “should have been an immediate non-starter,” and that the fight against the new railyard would continue. Both of the state's U.S. senators, Democrats Tammy Duckworth and Dick Durbin, called for transparency for the environmental review, but applauded the move as progress.</p><p>“We should not have had to scream, fight and pound on the doors of power just to get the basic transparency about the environmental effects this plan could have on our residents,” Lee said in a statement. “No matter what this environmental study produces, our concerns about noise pollution, economic impact and other issues remain unaddressed.”</p><p>Hannah Dembosky, founder of the Bridgeport Environmentalists, said she and other residents are still pushing for a more detailed Environmental Impact Statement. Demobosky is concerned the Trump administration’s history of flouting environmental concerns will carry through the Amtrak project’s two-month assessment.</p><p>She also hopes for an independent review of the findings. The Rail Passengers Association, a rail travel advocacy group based in Washington D.C., said it plans such a review, in addition to conducting its <a class="Link" href="http://www.railpassengers.org/canalyardsurvey" target="_blank" ><u>own community survey</u></a>.</p><p>“I am concerned that under the Trump administration, this environmental assessment could just be used to silence community members if it's done behind closed doors,” said Dembosky, a Bridgeport resident. “Having this next to so many homes, residences and schools, it'll be important to have detailed and accurate information.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-100000" entries.title: Top mayoral aides defend Mayor Johnson's tax-heavy $17.6B budget
entries.summary: <p>Top mayoral aides on Monday began their defense of Mayor Brandon Johnson’s tax-heavy <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/20/mayor-brandon-johnson-failed-corporate-head-tax-resurrected-proposed-budget" >$17.6 billion budget</a> and acknowledged that they have no Plan B, if as expected, the failed corporate head tax is shot down again.</p><p></p><p>One year after a 31-member coalition of conservative and moderate alderpersons rejected the mayor’s corporate head tax, 29 alderpersons have vowed to do the same with Johnson’s newest attempt. </p><p>They will be joined by business leaders, who are also determined to block the third and biggest increase yet involving a Chicago tax on equipment rentals and cloud computing. The current tax is already the highest in the nation.</p><p>Against that backdrop, Johnson’s finance team began the task of trying to sell a tax-the-rich budget that includes $664.2 million in new and increased taxes and $119.8 million in spending cuts. The trimming is even less, given the fact that up to $68 million of that spending is being shifted from the city’s corporate fund to enterprise funds.</p><p>“This budget is quote, unquote 'balanced’ with more than $5 in new revenue for every one dollar saved,” said 42nd Ward Ald. Brendan Reilly. “Why is the administration choosing taxing over managing its expenses?”</p><p>Acting Budget Director Jonathan Ernst said cost-cutting in Johnson’s first three budgets produced “nearly three-quarters of a billion dollars” in savings. “Those reductions continue this year. We’re adding another $120 million,” Ernst said.</p><p>Reilly was not appeased and lashed out at newly appointed Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch, a former senior director and mid-central regional manager at Fitch, the Wall Street rating agency that dropped Chicago’s bond rating in February to three notches above junk. </p><p>“This budget repeats every one of those problems listed by Fitch ratings where you once worked,” Reilly said. “We have at least $155.6 million in one-time money, $480 million in new borrowing for settlements, (a) $882 million structural gap and a jobs tax that a majority of this City Council rejected once already.”</p><p>Ninth Ward Ald. Anthony Beale demanded to know why the head tax was even presented to the City Council “knowing you had 29 aldermen who wouldn’t support it.”</p><p>“What’s Plan B if the head tax doesn’t pass?” Beale asked Ernst.</p><p>Ernst said, “Work with the City Council. We presented you with our plan.”</p><p>Eleventh Ward Ald. Nicole Lee, who helped lead last year’s unprecedented budget rebellion, homed in on Johnson’s proposal to raise by 33% the tax on equipment rentals, software and cloud computing.</p><p>“This is just an insane amount to increase the PPLT,” Lee said of the personal property lease transaction tax.</p><p>Lee said a promise was built into the management ordinance tied to the city’s 2026 budget that promised not to raise the so-called “cloud tax” for two years.</p><p>“What happened to the freeze, guys?” she asked.</p><p>Ernst said the two-year freeze was stricken from the management ordinance because the cloud tax has over-performed, and the city could not resist the temptation to take even greater advantage of what has become a cash cow.</p><p>“This is where the economy is moving toward, away from areas that we typically tax," Ernst said. "We need to evolve with that or else we don’t end up getting the structural fixes that we need.” </p><p>Johnson's decision to freeze hundreds of police vacancies and civilianize more than 130 more police jobs was another flash point on the first day of budget hearings. So was the mayor's plan to borrow $480 million over what Gabrysch described as five to seven years to cover settlements tied to allegations of police abuse. </p><p>The mayor recently used his fourth veto to block an ordinance that would have required a three-fifths vote for future borrowing. City Comptroller Michael Belsky denied that continued borrowing to cover operating costs would trigger another drop in the city's bond rating.</p><p>"These are things that happened years ago, that are now coming home to roost," Belsky said.</p><p>"We don't want this liability. Nobody does. But the best way to deal with it without crowding out a lot of services at that larger number and affecting the quality of life in Chicago — the only option you have is to finance ... as short as possible and you hope that, going into the future, these things dissipate so you don't have to face that floating liability every year."</p><p>Finance Chair and 3rd Ward Ald. Pat Dowell also made it clear that she and her colleagues would not allow Johnson to use the $75 million up-front payment they negotiated with Stonepeak Partners to be used toward the advanced pension payment. They want the $75 million to be an extra payment to chip away at the city's $36 billion pension crisis. That negotiation paved the way for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/29/city-council-parking-meters-deal-compromise-stonepeak-partners" >Stonepeak’s acquisition</a> of the city's parking meters. </p>

entries.title: Chicago police investigating potential misuse of other agencies' license plate reader systems
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Police Department is conducting an audit to determine whether cops abused their access to other law enforcement agencies’ license plate reader systems.</p><p>The audit comes with a slew of immediate and proposed policy changes to the way Chicago police officers are allowed to access license plate reader data.</p><p>The department said it has immediately reduced access to the outside license plate reader systems to only those whose “position and job duties” require access.</p><p>Each of the department’s five bureaus also will be required to designate someone to oversee the use of license plate reader systems, not only those owned by the department but also those owned by outside agencies.</p><p>Among the proposed changes, the department said it will make login information for the system non-transferable — meaning only one department member can use their log-in credentials — and require that a "legitimate law enforcement purpose” be documented for every query.</p><p>Additionally, monthly audits of searches would be conducted and the Office of Public Safety Administration would be tasked with processing requests by officers for access to outside license plate reader systems.</p><p>The proposal also outlines potential penalties for violations of the department’s directive, which range from suspension from use of the license plate reader search systems to referral for prosecution.</p><p>The department didn’t respond to questions about what initiated the audit or when the subsequent audits would be completed, but said in an earlier statement that the technology plays a “vital role” in homicide, shooting and missing persons cases.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson's office declined to comment due to the ongoing nature of the audit.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagopolice.org/policy-review/cpd-automated-license-plate-reader-alpr-systems/" target="_blank" ><u>draft</u></a> of the department’s new policy regarding license plate reader use is <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagopolice.org/policy-review/cpd-automated-license-plate-reader-alpr-systems/" target="_blank" ><u>open for public comment</u></a> through Nov. 12. The department said it will “review the additional feedback received to guide future revisions to the draft” before finalizing the directives.</p><p>CPD is the latest local law enforcement agency to announce internal inquiries into possible abuses of license plate reader technology amid public outcry against surveillance technology company Flock Safety.</p><p>Earlier this month, a former Joliet police lieutenant was hit with felony charges for alleged misuse of Flock technology. It is the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/01/illinois-cities-halt-flock-use-suspend-officers-and-review-policy-amid-alleged-improper-use" target="_blank" ><u>third known case this year of a Will County law enforcement officer being accused of misusing the database</u></a> that tracks millions of drivers’ real-time locations.</p><p>Officers from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/06/former-itasca-west-chicago-police-officers-charged-over-alleged-misuse-of-flock-cameras" target="_blank" ><u>Itasca</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/06/former-itasca-west-chicago-police-officers-charged-over-alleged-misuse-of-flock-cameras" target="_blank" ><u>West Chicago</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/27/flock-license-plate-reader-alpr-chicago-suburb" target="_blank" ><u>Prairie Grove</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/27/flock-license-plate-reader-alpr-chicago-suburb" target="_blank" ><u>Kenosha County, Wisconsin</u></a><u>,</u> have all been hit with felony charges following their alleged misuse of the cameras and databases. The Will County sheriff’s office and Channahon Police Department <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/01/illinois-cities-halt-flock-use-suspend-officers-and-review-policy-amid-alleged-improper-use" target="_blank" ><u>have also suspended officers</u></a> pending investigations into the searches.</p><p>On Nov. 12, the Will County Board <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/07/former-joliet-police-officer-charged-over-alleged-flock-camera-misuse" target="_blank" ><u>is set to consider</u></a> an ordinance to ban automated license plate reader cameras on county property. That's the same day public comment closes for the updated CPD directive.</p>

entries.title: Por miedo a ICE, algunos inmigrantes de Chicago cambian su trabajo y vida diaria a horas nocturnas
entries.summary: <p>Antes de salir de su casa, incluso para ir a lavar la ropa a una lavandería cercana, Gustavo Domínguez reza. Le pide a Dios que lo deje regresar a casa sano y salvo.</p><p>Era de noche cuando Domínguez, de 49 años de edad, y su esposa Patricia Dávila, de 67, cargaron sus bolsas de ropa en la cajuela y salieron. Domínguez no tiene estatus legal. Su esposa tiene autorización de trabajo y dice que solicitó asilo tras huir de amenazas en México.</p><p>Ahora esperan hasta la noche para lavar la ropa y hacer compras. Tienen miedo de toparse con agentes del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) durante el día.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fe0000" name="module-fe0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>En la lavandería, Domínguez descarga apresuradamente las bolsas. Dávila ayuda y habla mientras trabaja. Dávila ha notado que ahora mucha más gente viene a lavar por la noche.</p><p>“Ahorita vas a ver que más tarde empieza a llegar más gente”, dice Dávila.</p><p>Una vez puesta la lavadora, la pareja sale a comprar en un supermercado cercano mientras la oscuridad se instala en el vecindario.</p><p>Adentro, piñatas cuelgan del techo. Ollas gigantes de tamales ocupan una repisa alta junto a unas hieleras. Cada uno empuja un carrito, cubriendo distintas partes de la tienda para terminar las compras más rápido.</p><p>Dávila dice que a menudo ve a jóvenes en videollamadas con sus madres, mostrando productos y preguntando qué marca comprar.</p><p>Hay “tanto miedo que mandan a los muchachos a hacer las compras”, afirma.</p><p>Casi un año después de que el Operativo Midway Blitz terminara oficialmente, los inmigrantes en Chicago siguen cambiando sus horarios de trabajo y haciendo las diligencias cotidianas en las horas nocturnas o antes del amanecer por miedo a ser arrestados o detenidos por ICE.</p><p>Trabajadores describieron comprar insumos para vender antes del amanecer, trabajar de noche, hacer compras nocturnas y reducir las salidas de sus casas. Algunos todavía trabajan de día porque dependen de esos ingresos, pero cambian sus horarios cuando pueden. Ese cambio ha significado una pérdida de ingresos y la ansiedad constante sigue afectando la salud mental y las relaciones.</p><h3>‘Gente de la noche’</h3><p>Desde comienzos de 2026 hasta la primera semana de agosto, ICE realizó 1,560 arrestos en el Condado de Cook, según un análisis del Chicago Sun-Times y WBEZ de datos de detenciones de ICE obtenidos por el Deportation Data Project. Grupos legales y comunitarios han documentado encuentros en cortes, escuelas y supermercados, y dicen que los operativos se han vuelto menos publicitados pero siguen ocurriendo como parte de la campaña de deportaciones masivas en curso de la administración de Trump.</p><p>“Nos estamos convirtiendo en gente de la noche”, dice Baltazar Enríquez, presidente del Concilio Comunitario de La Villita. “Ahora hacemos las cosas de noche”.</p><p>Enríquez dice conocer a muchos inmigrantes que adoptaron el turno nocturno como forma de intentar evitar encuentros con ICE. Una madre le dijo que le cuesta dormir después de trabajar de noche. Todavía tiene que alistar a sus hijos por la mañana cuando llega a casa. Él recordó que ella describía periodos de solo dos o tres horas de descanso, tomando siestas cuando podía.</p><p>“Me están saliendo ojeras” le dijo, según Enríquez.</p><p>Rosemary Magaña, terapeuta y directora de programas de la Coalición por la Salud Mental de los Inmigrantes, dice que las rutinas nocturnas pueden costarle a la gente las conexiones sociales que les ayudan a sobrellevar la situación. Las visitas, las salidas de fin de semana y las reuniones desaparecen.</p><p>Magaña ha sentido esa vigilancia en carne propia. Durante los primeros días de Midway Blitz, regresaba de llevar a su hijo a la escuela y pasaba el tiempo mirando coches e imaginando qué haría si los agentes los paraban. Una vez, dice, su cuello se puso tan rígido que no podía moverlo.</p><h3>Los agentes impulsaron la nueva rutina nocturna</h3><p>Dávila dice que sus nuevas rutinas nocturnas comenzaron después de que vieron a agentes de inmigración detener gente cerca de su casa. En un incidente el otoño pasado, los agentes pasaron cerca de sus ventanas mientras una niña en una patineta les advertía a los vecinos que no salieran. Los agentes la derribaron de la patineta, según Domínguez, quien dice que escuchó fuertes estallidos y que cayeron botes de gas lacrimógeno detrás de su casa y frente a la de un vecino.</p><p>Domínguez cubrió las ventanas con cobijas. Cerraron las puertas con llave y apagaron las luces. Temía que los agentes entraran. Entre septiembre y parte de octubre de 2025, intentaron quedarse en casa. Durante aproximadamente un mes, una amiga con estatus legal llevaba a Patricia a lavar la ropa y a comprar. Gustavo siguió yendo a trabajar, pero dejó de manejar.</p><p>Durante esos primeros meses de Midway Blitz, pagó viajes en Uber al trabajo, a veces acostándose en el asiento trasero. Domínguez trabaja en un almacén y carga camiones. Cuando su turno terminaba, esperaba horas a que un compañero lo llevara a casa. Otro Uber costaba demasiado.</p><p>Se puso ansioso y perdió peso, quizá entre 10 y 20 libras, dice Patricia. Se preocupa por él.</p><p>Dávila huyó de amenazas de muerte en México después de denunciar abusos sexuales a niñas y ayudar a personas a escapar de la violencia. En 2010, dos de sus sobrinos fueron asesinados en una masacre estudiantil. Ahora teme quedarse en Chicago y regresar a México.</p><p>“Estoy en medio de dos fuegos”, dice.</p><p>Aun así, atribuye a su participación en organizaciones comunitarias el haberle dado cierto sentido de protección cuando todo se vuelve abrumador.</p><p>Pero ve a su esposo batallando más con el miedo, todavía ansioso y enojado por lo que presenciaron el otoño pasado.</p><p>Gustavo tiene una camiseta de un equipo deportivo de Estados Unidos que ya no puede ponerse.</p><p>“La admiración que yo sentía por este país se ha convertido en un desprecio”, dice.</p><p>Habla de ver a padres maltratados por agentes delante de sus hijos, del dolor que los niños podrían llevar mucho tiempo después de una detención.</p><p>“Eres su héroe, ¿y te tratan así?” dice. “Lo que quieren es arrancarte la dignidad”.</p><p>Además de la ansiedad, hay presiones económicas. La pareja ha apartado suficiente dinero para pagar aproximadamente dos meses de renta en caso de que uno de los dos sea detenido.</p><p>Antes iban al centro comercial por ropa y otras cosas que necesitaban, dice Patricia. Ahora pide más por internet, comprando ropa en el sitio Shein y artículos del hogar y personales por Amazon. Comprar así puede salir más caro, afirma. Extraña encontrar ofertas en persona.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2f6339" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Patricia Dávila dice que sus nuevas rutinas nocturnas comenzaron después de que vieron a agentes de inmigración detener a personas cerca de su casa un día del otoño pasado.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Pérdida de sueño</h3><p>En el sistema hospitalario Cook County Health, el psiquiatra Dr. Hugo Solari escucha a diario a pacientes que viven con miedo a ICE.</p><p>“Todos los días, en la consulta, oigo a pacientes hablar de cómo tuvieron que adaptar sus vidas para evitar encontrarse con ICE”, dice Solari.</p><p>Algunos piden citas por telemedicina o recetas por correo. Otros posponen la atención preventiva por temor a salir de casa.</p><p>El estrés también interrumpe el sueño. La ansiedad dificulta dormir y la falta de sueño profundiza la ansiedad. Para pacientes que trasladan sus actividades a la noche, conseguir sueño suficiente y regular puede volverse aún más difícil. Con el tiempo, dice Solari, el estrés crónico y el sueño interrumpido pueden afectar la salud física además de la mental.</p><h3>Mover el trabajo a la noche</h3><p>Imelda, una cuidadora de niños que no tiene estatus legal, ahora sólo acepta trabajos de niñera por la noche. Imelda es un apodo. El Sun-Times no usa su nombre real porque ella teme la deportación.</p><p>Se siente muy orgullosa de su trabajo, enseñar a los niños a tratar a los demás. Disfruta especialmente cuidar a menores de 3 años.</p><p>“Me gusta sembrarles empatía, respeto, por todas las personas”, dice.</p><p>Cuando comenzaron los operativos de inmigración el otoño pasado, Imelda cuidaba a una niña. Aún la llevaba a museos, parques y la biblioteca, vigilando por agentes en el camino. Niñeras se llamaban entre sí para avisarse sobre agentes adonde llevaban a los niños, pidiendo a sus compañeras evitar esas áreas y cuidarse.</p><p>Pero en el trabajo, Imelda trató de no mostrar su miedo.</p><p>“Y con todo el cuerpo temblando tenía que ser profesional en mi trabajo”, dice.</p><p>Le contó a la madre de la niña lo asustada que se sentía. Su empleadora cambió la organización de su trabajo. La familia también le ofreció refugio a ella y su familia en su casa. La oferta la hizo sentir valorada y cuidada.</p><p>La recordó a Ana Frank.</p><p>Ese trabajo terminó cuando la niña empezó la escuela. Ahora, Imelda acepta cuidados esporádicos por la noche, ayudando a los niños con la cena, el baño, los libros y la hora de dormir. El trabajo la mantiene dentro de casa, pero trabaja apenas unas dos veces al mes.</p><p>Imelda se consideraba alguien a quien los demás podían recurrir. A través de su voluntariado en derechos laborales, representa a la gente y alza la voz por ellos. Entre sus compañeras, ella es la que canta, baila y trata de relajar a todos. Pero últimamente se sorprende de su propio miedo, de lo difícil que le resulta salir de casa.</p><p>Pero ni siquiera quedarse en casa apaga el miedo.</p><p>Los pasos arriba le hacen pensar que los agentes han entrado al edificio. Se imagina a alguien dejándolos entrar. Considera dónde podría esconderse. Afuera, estudia los coches que pasan por si podrían pertenecer a agentes de inmigración.</p><p>Magaña, la terapeuta, dice que la ansiedad prolongada puede cambiar lo que la gente espera del mundo. Anticipan peligro y dudan de que las circunstancias vayan a mejorar. Ella lo describe como trauma sistémico, que alcanza más allá de quienes son detenidos directamente.</p><p>“No tiene que pasarte a ti para que te traumatice”, dice.</p><p>Imelda trata de mantenerse fuerte por sus hijos y asegurarles que no pasará nada. Pero ellos también tienen miedo, dice. Las salidas al parque y el tiempo de juego al aire libre se han vuelto menos frecuentes. Le preocupa que los niños asuman preocupaciones por la comida y la renta cuando deberían poder concentrarse en sus estudios.</p><p>“Todo esto va a tener consecuencias y yo lo estoy viendo más en nuestros hijos”, dice.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c9c5dc" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Guillermo Flores atiende a sus clientes. A veces se queda en casa y no trabaja si teme un encuentro con ICE.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Compras antes del amanecer</h3><p>Guillermo Flores, de 54 años de edad, fue uno de los primeros en llegar a la reunión mensual de la Asociación de Vendedores Ambulantes. Tomó asiento mientras otros vendedores iban llegando.</p><p>Flores ha vendido comida desde un carrito por unos 16 años. Prepara vasos de mango, sandía, piña y pepino antes de salir con raspados, frituras y chicharrones.</p><p>Tiene licencia para vender y paga impuestos, dice. Tiene licencia de conducir desde hace más de 14 años sin accidentes ni revocaciones.</p><p>“Estoy tratando de hacer todo correcto”, dice.</p><p>Aun así, los reportes de acciones de inmigración en su vecindario a menudo lo mantienen sin vender. Se queda en casa un día, a veces otro, perdiendo ingresos.</p><p>Evitar trabajar de día por completo significaría renunciar al negocio que ha construido durante años. En cambio, cambia las partes del día que puede. Solía comprar la despensa alrededor de las 7 a.m. Ahora hace las compras a las 5, antes del amanecer, con la esperanza de evitar un encuentro. Sigue vendiendo durante el día, pero menos horas.</p><p>Algunos vendedores prefieren trabajar cerca unos de otros para poder ayudarse y intercambiar avisos, dice. Donde él vende, solo hay otro vendedor cerca.</p><p>Para Flores, mover sus horas de venta a la noche traería un riesgo distinto. Teme los asaltos y evita quedarse afuera después de oscurecer.</p><p>“Nos tenemos que cuidar de ICE y también nos tenemos que cuidar de los robos”, dice.</p><p>Cuando ve que se hace de noche, se va.</p><p>“Le doy gracias a Dios y lo que se vendió, se vendió, y vámonos”, afirma.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Rosemary Magaña, terapeuta y directora de programas de la Coalición para la Salud Mental de los Inmigrantes, dice que las rutinas nocturnas pueden hacer que las personas pierdan conexiones sociales que les ayudan a sobrellevar. Visitas, salidas de fin de semana y reuniones se van perdiendo.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Buscar apoyo</h3><p>Magaña escucha a mujeres especialmente que cuidan de todos los demás mientras ocultan su propio malestar. Les preocupa que mostrarse asustadas asuste también a sus hijos.</p><p>“Puedes llorar y sufrir y también ayudar a los demás”, dice.</p><p>El apoyo comienza por que te crean, añade Magaña.</p><p>“Busca espacios que te crean, que validen y normalicen tu estrés”, dice. “Que no te llamen paranoica”.</p><p>Una sesión semanal de terapia no siempre es suficiente. Habló de cocinar juntas, compartir comida y encontrar personas que escuchen sin minimizar el peligro. La coalición ofrece <a class="Link" href="https://www.ourcimh.org/" target="_blank" >círculos virtuales de apoyo gratuitos</a> para inmigrantes y quienes los acompañan.</p><p>“Estoy aquí para apoyarte en lo que vaya a funcionar mejor para ti”, dice.</p><p>De vuelta en el supermercado, Patricia y Gustavo encuentran una fila más corta en la caja registradora y se unen rápidamente. Su ropa sigue en la lavandería. Tienen que regresar y secarla antes de poder volver a casa.</p><p>Para esas diligencias, van juntos. Pero el trabajo los lleva por rumbos distintos.</p><p>En el trabajo, Patricia limpia habitaciones de hotel mientras espera el texto de Gustavo confirmando que ha llegado a su trabajo en el almacén a las 10 a m. Si su mensaje no llega a la hora de siempre, le dijo, ella debe entender que lo han detenido.</p><p>Antes rara vez enviaba mensajes de texto. Ahora, Patricia ha guardado un año de sus mensajes diarios:</p><p>“Ya llegué”.</p><p><i>Contribuyó: Keenan Chen </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: All 4 NFC North teams are playoff-caliber — and have fatal flaws
entries.summary: <p>Matt LaFleur didn’t want to make a bad day worse by getting fined. So when the Packers coach was asked Sunday about the controversial calls during their 20-17 loss to the division rival Lions, he went full Marshawn Lynch.</p><p>“I can say what I really think, but I don't think it does any good,” he said. “So, it is what it is. You’ve just got to overcome it.”</p><p>The Packers had the chance to move beyond two roughing the passer flags — including one of the game-winning drive — and an unnecessary roughness call in which the official who threw the flag did so while lying on his back after getting knocked over by players after he believed the play had ended. It was as simple as making their field goals.</p><p>Trey Smack, though, missed a 26-yarder in the first quarter and had a 35-yarder tipped in the fourth. He missed from 43 and 47 yards two weeks ago against the Bears. No one in the NFL has missed more kicks than Smack’s five this year.</p><p>It’s the perfect encapsulation of the NFC North through seven weeks. It’s the best division in football — and each team, including the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>, comes with glaring flaws.</p><p>That’s at once encouraging and a challenge to be solved over the next three months. All four teams can, with a straight face, say that they have Super Bowl aspirations. Whether on the field or in general manager conversations — the league’s trade deadline is two weeks from Tuesday — they’ll be racing each other for position.</p><p>Were the season to end today, all four NFC North teams would make the playoffs, with the undefeated Vikings earning a bye and the Bears, Lions and Packers serving as seeds 5-7. Since the NFL switched to four-team division in 2002, no division has ever sent all four teams to the postseason.</p><p>None of the four are perfect. Particularly the team on top.</p><p>The Vikings are the last undefeated team in the NFL. They have the best defense in the league. Their offense, though, is more pedestrian than a crosswalk. They’re fourth-worst in the NFL in yards and passing yards. Entering Monday night’s game, their 20.8 points per game were third-worst in the NFC. Kyler Murray has improved — but he’s had a worse passer rating in each of the last two weeks than J.J. McCarthy, whom the Vikings traded away to the Giants for a song last month.</p><p>The Vikings’ 16-10 win against the Colts on Sunday marked the fourth time this year an NFL team has emerged victorious despite scoring 16 or fewer points and 275 or fewer yards. The Vikings have done it twice, including Week 2 against the Bears.</p><p>The Bears’ flaw made its appearance Thursday just as fans were celebrating what felt like the start of a blowout victory. With the Bears ahead by 13 and three seconds left in the first half, they blitzed Patriots quarterback Drake Maye at the New England 48. Maye dumped the ball off to running back Rhamondre Stevenson, who sprinted up the right sideline for a touchdown. He was touched once — Jaylon Johnson nicked his undershirt.</p><p>Out of the 76 cornerbacks who have played at least half their team’s snaps, Johnson has the fifth-worst coverage grade, per Pro Football Focus. Rookie Malik Muhammad has the 15<sup>th</sup>-worst.</p><p>The Bears give up 20.4 points per game, the ninth-fewest in the NFL. They can look dominant at times, thanks to a killer third-down package and coordinator Dennis Allen’s knack for exotic blitzes. But what happens when the Bears can’t get to the passer? What happens when those blitzes don’t land? What happens when Allen’s gambles don’t pay off?</p><p>Dan Campbell certainly knows that feeling — though he was lucky not to experience it Sunday. The Lions coach decided to for it twice on fourth down, costing his team points the first time and, were it not for some good fortune, the game on the second.</p><p>With about a minute left in the third quarter and the Lions up by three, Campbell called a pass play on fourth-and-goal from the Packers’ 6 rather than kick a field goal. It failed.</p><p>Then Campbell got absolutely ridiculous. With about five minutes left in a tied game, he went for it on fourth-and-one — from his own 24. Jahmyr Gibbs was stuffed for a two-yard loss. Then Smack had his field goal tipped four plays later.</p><p>Campbell explained his rationale with two points: he thought they’d make it, and he knew they’d get the ball back regardless. By that rationale, then, he should have just handed the Packers the ball and told them to score.</p><p>The Lions give up more yards per game in football. Their coach leads the league in hubris. If the former doesn’t doom them, the latter might.</p><p>Not that the Lions were apologizing after kicking their own field goal as time expired to win their first NFC North game of the year.</p><p><b>“</b>They all count the same,”quarterback Jared Goff said, “if we play this game now or later in the year with the division on the line .”</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: White Sox announce John Schriffen won't return as TV voice
entries.summary: <p>For John Schriffen, it's three seasons and you're out.</p><p>The White Sox announced Monday that Schriffen won't return to their TV booth next season. The team said it told Schriffen, 42, that it won't extend his contract. His three-year deal expired after the season, and the Sox won't pick up the option year.</p><p>The move comes as no surprise after Schriffen's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2025/09/18/white-sox-john-schriffen-steve-stone-gordon-beckham-chicago-sports-network-mike-mccarthy-marquee-sports-network" target="_blank" >rocky run as the play-by-play voice</a>. His defense of the Sox during their record 121-loss season in 2024 was outlandish, and his lack of baseball-broadcasting experience and knowledge of the franchise were apparent. Yet, his excitement endeared him to a segment of Sox fans, particularly during the team's playoff run this season. </p><p>“John has been a true professional throughout his three seasons with the White Sox, bringing energy, enthusiasm and a distinctive style to our broadcasts," Brooks Boyer, the Sox' chief revenue and marketing officer, said in a statement. </p><p>"As his contract comes to an end, we believe this is the appropriate time to evaluate the direction of our broadcasts and determine what is best for the organization and our fans moving forward. We are appreciative of John’s contributions and the connection he built with our fan base. We wish him continued success in his future endeavors.”</p><p>"I’m grateful to the Chicago White Sox organization for the opportunity to call games over the past three seasons," Schriffen said. "Being part of this team’s turnaround and playoff run was truly special. I want to thank White Sox fans for welcoming me to Chicago and for their support throughout my time here. I’ll always cherish the memories and look forward to what’s next."</p><p>Perhaps Schriffen saw the writing on the wall <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/10/15/john-schriffen-chicago-white-sox-tv-steve-stone-connor-mcknight-connor-onion-wayne-randazzo-len-kasper-darrin-jackson" target="_blank" >when he chose to call a UFC event</a> rather than be available for the Sox' playoff clincher in September. Schriffen contractually was allowed a certain number of games off, but his decision to miss the Sox' first clinching game in five years couldn't have sat well with team brass.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Why I can't figure out how seriously to take the Blackhawks' bad start — or what to expect next
entries.summary: <p>I have a confession to make: I'm not sure how to analyze the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> right now.</p><p>Oh, they've been bad so far. I can tell you that. I could provide many stats as supporting evidence, too, but the standings suffice well enough. At 3-8-0, the Hawks have the second-worst record in the NHL.</p><p>I'm struggling to identify who deserves the bulk of the blame for the team's woes, though. </p><p>Is it general manager Kyle Davidson, who assembled this roster? Is it coach Jeff Blashill and his staff, whose systems don't seem to be working well? Or is it the players, who have been universally mistake-prone on the ice?</p><p>I'm also struggling to determine how problematic it is that they've been bad. Perhaps these early-season struggles were inevitable with a roster this young and recently assembled, or perhaps they're an indication this roster will never succeed.</p><p>And I'm really struggling to predict what will happen the rest of the season.</p><p>Perhaps Blashill's seat will heat up by January or February. That could then heat up Davidson's seat, since not many GMs get the privilege to hire and fire more than two different coaches.</p><p>Perhaps Hawks chairman Danny Wirtz's confidence in Davidson — whom he just awarded a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/15/blackhawks-kyle-davidson-contract-extension-danny-wirtz" >contract extension</a> in April — and patience with the slow rebuilding plan will hold strong. That could allow Davidson to maintain his belief in and patience with Blashill and keep fans' impatient (in some cases furious) cries falling on deaf ears. </p><p>Or perhaps the Hawks are about to turn things around — like the equally young Sharks did around this time last season — and all questions about seat temperatures will fade away naturally.</p><p>I would love to anticipate which hypothetical path will become reality, so I've been searching for any sorts of signals hidden within the first month of the season. </p><p>Every attempt to do so, however, ignites a tug-of-war between different thought processes in my brain. Here's how it usually goes:</p><p><i>The Hawks' results need to be taken with grains of salt because their schedule has been brutal. Almost every opponent has been a Stanley Cup contender. Plus, they've only played one game with both their No. 1 forward (Connor Bedard) and presumptive No. 1 defenseman (Bowen Byram) in the lineup.</i></p><p><i>But in hockey, bad teams should still beat good teams sometimes. The Predators just walloped the Avalanche 6-2 on Sunday. The Hawks haven't done that even once yet. Every team deals with injuries, too. And quantity-wise, the Hawks haven't actually had that many.</i></p><p><i>But the Hawks have been snakebitten. Their past three games (in which they've scored three goals) have been laden with missed opportunities. That should even out over time.</i></p><p><i>But most teams think they're unlucky — because scoring is really difficult. The Hawks' team shooting percentage (10.2%) is only one tick off league average. Meanwhile, they're 31st in shots on goal per game, and that's not luck.</i></p><p><i>But Blashill is a smart coach. He possesses the right combination of intelligence and flexibility to succeed tactically and the right combination of empathy and assertiveness to succeed developmentally. Many fans have convinced themselves otherwise, but he's impressive in-person.</i></p><p><i>But every NHL coach is smart and well-rounded. The bar is high in this league. And clearly Blashill's systems aren't working as intended, regardless of whose fault it is. The Hawks often look lost in defensive-zone coverage, have been awful with defensive-zone breakouts and haven't been effective on the forecheck.</i></p><p><i>But young studs like Anton Frondell, Roman Kantserov and Artyom Levshunov have already shown flashes of immense talent and should get more comfortable in the NHL over time. They have the potential to become stars alongside Bedard, and a few stars can dramatically change a team.</i></p><p><i>But it could take them a couple more years to reach stardom, and nobody wants to wait a couple more years — especially for outcomes that aren't guaranteed. That would be excruciating.</i></p><p><i>But my own expectation bias probably influences my perspective. I'm so accustomed to watching the Hawks lose (after covering five consecutive terrible seasons) that it's difficult for me to imagine them winning. </i></p><p><i>But that track record of losing genuinely can create a cycle that's difficult to escape. Confidence is real, and not only do the Hawks lack it relative to their peers, but opposing teams have good reasons to feel extra confident against them. Climbing a mountain is harder than defending it from the top.</i></p><p>I imagine most Hawks fans aren't encountering the same endless mental loop. I've already heard from many with fully formed strong opinions. </p><p>Most fans are affected by emotions, however. Take emotion out, and the logic — at least to me — balances on both sides.</p><p>The brutal-schedule element isn't about to stop complicating the evaluation process, either. After a brief respite against the Kings and Red Wings, the Hawks will enter another six-game murderer's row against Cup contenders. Things won't lighten up until the second half of November.</p><p>Conclusions generally become safer to draw as sample sizes get larger, however, so I'm hopeful the next few weeks will show me some light. I'll keep searching for signals in the meantime.</p>
